item.title: 20分鐘深度認識現代京都！400年前的五天「寬永行幸」盛典 為何讓花街、歌舞伎保留下來？
item.itunes:title: 20分鐘深度認識現代京都！400年前的五天「寬永行幸」盛典 為何讓花街、歌舞伎保留下來？
item.itunes:author: 工頭堅。旅行長
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OdOfyIE0cpY

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入了解京都「寬永行幸」400週年背後，皇室與幕府如何透過盛事推動璀璨的寬永文化與工藝巔峰。
  • 探尋日本傳統「歌舞伎」從出雲阿國的前衛河原演出，一路演變至今日四條南座劇場的歷史脈絡。
  • 釐清祇園與先斗町等知名「花街」因參拜信仰與運河商貿而生的不同淵源，並認識藝妓與舞妓的文化制度。

摘要

寬永行幸：牽動江戶初期文化繁盛的世紀盛事

說書人工頭堅指出，2026年京都將迎來寬永行幸400週年紀念。回溯至1626年，退位將軍德川秀忠與三代將軍德川家光邀請後水尾天皇行幸二條城展開為期五天的盛會。彼時大坂之陣剛落幕不久，政治重心雖已轉移至江戶，但幕府藉由迎請兼具親屬關係的天皇，展現政權穩定並促進公武融和。二條城為此大幅擴建與彩繪裝飾，匯聚了頂尖畫師、詩人、樂師與工藝匠人，這場世紀盛會不僅展示了豐厚的文化底蘊，亦催生了後世所稱的寬永文化，而平民百姓在街道夾道觀看的身影，也悄然拉開了江戶市井娛樂生活蓬勃發展的序幕。

出雲阿國的創新舞步：歌舞伎與四條河原町的繁榮

與此同時，京都的民間娛樂亦迎來劃時代的變革。1603年德川家康就任征夷大將軍之際，出雲阿國在京都開創了前衛且略帶叛逆風格的舞作，成為現代歌舞伎的起源。阿國女扮男裝、身著華服進行逗趣演出，吸引大量觀眾駐足於神社與四條河原町的臨時舞台。隨著幕府後續頒令禁止女性與少年登台，歌舞伎逐漸演變成由成年男性專職扮演的傳統形式。四條一帶曾經林立的七座劇場，歷經火災與更迭後，如今僅存南座延續香火；而觀賞戲劇所帶動的餐飲、道具製作與住宿需求，更奠定了四條河原町繁盛的商業網絡。

水運與信仰交織：祇園、先斗町花街與藝妓文化

沿著劇場周邊蔓延的生活圈進一步孕育了京都獨特的花街文化。工頭堅分析，祇園最初是為八坂神社進香客提供茶水休息的「水茶屋」，因需求擴大而漸漸轉型為擁有幕府營業許可的花街；而先斗町則夾在鴨川與高瀨川之間，依托著高瀨川的水運樞紐聚集舟船工與各地客商，進而發展出茶屋、旅社與藝能空間。兩地因地理與客群不同而展現相異風貌，並確立了由成年的藝妓與見習階段的舞妓組成的傳承體系，茶屋更依循「不接生客」的信用制度維持宴席品質，使江戶時代的生活風貌在今日京都窄巷間依然歷久彌新。

================================================

# 寬永行幸四百年，京都從哪裡來

Hello everyone, I’m your travel guide , Gong Tou-Jian. On December 6, 2026, Kyoto plans to reenact the procession of the Emperor traveling to Nijo Castle 400 years ago. Why would a journey that lasted only five days back then be commemorated so solemnly 400 years later? How did the familiar Kabuki theaters, Hanamachi districts, teahouses, and ryokan we visit in Kyoto today gradually take shape? My sequel to the widely loved "Kyoto Time," titled "Gong Tou-Jian’s Kyoto Time II : Modern Era," has also just been released. As I continue to visit Kyoto,. I increasingly feel that much of the life experienced by today's travelers must be traced back to the Edo period. In this episode, we’ll look at the " 400th Anniversary of the Kan'ei Imperial Visit" to see how the people of Kyoto back then enjoyed theater, conducted business, and entertained guests, leading to the places where we can now buy tickets for performances, grab a coffee, or even stay overnight. If you enjoy this content, you are welcome to join the channel membership and walk further along this path with me. So, let’s...First of all...The. term "Gyoko" refers to an imperial visit. In 1626, the retired Shogun Tokugawa Hidetada and the third Shogun, Tokugawa Iemitsu, jointly welcomed Emperor Go-Mizunoo to Nijo Castle for a five-day stay. It had been only 11 years since the Siege of Osaka and the fall of the Toyotomi clan. The center of Japanese political operations had already shifted to Edo, but the Emperor and the Imperial Court remained in Kyoto, with Nijo Castle serving as the Shogun’s residence during his visits. The Shogun invited the Emperor to foster harmony, bringing feudal lords from across the country together to.

# 寬永行幸：將軍迎接天皇的五天

showcase the stability growing under Tokugawa rule through this grand event. There was also a family connection: the Emperor’s consort, Tokugawa Masako, was Hidetada’s daughter and Iemitsu’s sister, who later became known as Tofukumon-in. In other words, the people welcoming the Emperor were simultaneously his father-in-law and his brother-in-law. Of course, the power dynamic between the Court and the Shogunate did not mean that becoming in-laws ended all conflict. However, this time, let’s put the politics in the background and look at what Kyoto prepared for those five days. To host. the Emperor, the Shogunate expanded the castle, renovated the palaces and gardens, commissioned artists to paint wall murals, and arranged banquets, court music, Noh plays, and other cultural activities. Beyond painters, poets, and musicians, it was also necessary to prepare exquisite cuisine and various gifts. I have introduced the architecture of Nijo Castle before, so I won't go into detail here, but these preparations perfectly demonstrate just how much craftsmanship was gathered in Kyoto at that time. Emperor Go-Mizunoo himself loved poetry , tea, and flower arranging. Interactions between the imperial court. , nobility, temples, the samurai class, and wealthy merchants provided opportunities for painting, gardening, and crafts to flourish. The later " Kanei Culture" can be understood within this context, and this procession was a grand display of the cultural activities of the time. Interestingly, the "Nijo Castle Procession" screen painting depicts not only the procession itself but also the crowds watching along the route. While the Emperor and the Shogun were the stars of the ceremony, many ordinary people were also on the streets, leaving behind details of their lives in how. they dressed and watched the event. This autumn, the Sen-oku Hakuko Kan and The Museum of Kyoto are holding related exhibitions, while in December, the procession itself will be reenacted— these are two separate events. Thinking beyond the crowds in the screen painting, there are more stories of Kyoto life outside the court. For this, we must shift our focus back three years to the very beginning of the Edo period. In 1603, the same year Tokugawa Ieyasu was appointed Shogun, another.

# 阿國銅像與歌舞伎的起點

event with significant later influence took place in Kyoto: the performances of Izumo no Okuni began. Walking out from Shijo Station, near the Shijo Bridge, you can see a bronze statue of a woman. With a fan in one hand and a long sword slung behind her shoulder, her striking pose is that of Okuni. Many travelers pass by her on their way to the Minami-za theater, Hanamikoji, or the shrines. There is much uncertainty surrounding Okuni's life, but the performances she introduced are now considered the origins of Kabuki. Back then, the term "kabuki" carried a connotation of deviating from the norm and deliberately striking a different pose. She would dress as a man in flamboyant costumes, performing themes such as tea house entertainment and comedic roles, attracting large crowds to watch. When we think of Kabuki today , we might imagine formal theaters, traditional costumes, and actors from hereditary lineages, but in Okuni’s time, it was a form of entertainment that was even considered a bit daring. Many performances later labeled as " traditional" first drew attention precisely because they differed from. existing forms. However, the presence of a bronze statue by the bridge does not necessarily mean that Okuni’s first performance took place right at the foot of that statue. The "Okuni Kabuki" screen painting, held by the Kyoto National Museum, depicts her performing on a Noh stage at the Kitano Tenmangu Shrine. Performances at the time were likely held at shrines or on temporary stages in riverbeds, rather than in fixed, dedicated theater buildings. As the trend caught on and more groups began to imitate her, the Shijo riverbed grew increasingly lively . Later, the shogunate banned performances by women and youths, so.

actors became primarily adult males, and female roles were played by men, gradually developing the form we are familiar with today. In the Shijo-Kawaramachi area, there were seven authorized theaters during the early Edo period. Their names and locations shifted due to fires, renovations, and management changes, eventually leaving only the Minami-za and Kita-za. By the Meiji era, the Kita-za also closed, leaving only the Minami-za to continue performances today. If you walk over there, the name of the Kita-za still remains on the storefronts near Shijo Bridge, while. the Minami-za continues to hang its performance banners across Shijo-dori. Buying souvenirs, watching plays, and dining—the activities concentrated in this area today all have their own unique histories when you look back. Back then, for a theater to operate, the surrounding area needed places to eat and places for workers to rest. Actors required costumes, makeup, and props, and audiences would also look for places to dine after the show; the performances drew people, and the people brought business. Kyoto's entertainment life flourished amidst this constant flow. So. From here, one. can walk to the nearby hanamachi ( geisha districts). Although Kabuki actors, geiko, and maiko often appear together in the impressions foreign tourists have of Kyoto, their work and history are actually quite different. Kabuki is performed in theaters, while Kyoto’s geiko and maiko entertain guests at banquets with dance, music, and conversation. While there is a history of exchange between them, the hanamachi have their own distinct development process. The origins of the Gion district are linked to the area in front of today's Yasaka Shrine. Pilgrims needed tea and rest, leading.

# 祇園與先斗町，花街怎麼形成

to the creation of "water tea houses," which gradually began to offer more services as the number of guests and their needs grew. By the mid-Edo period , some tea houses obtained operating permits from the shogunate, and the hanamachi system we are familiar with today was gradually formed through these changes. As for the Ponto-cho area on the other side, it must be understood through its waterways. It is nestled between the Kamo River and the Takase River; the Takase River was used for transporting goods, attracting boatmen, merchants, and travelers to the vicinity. After the western bank of. the river was reclaimed, there was land available for development. Around 1712, tea houses and inns—places for socializing and lodging—began to appear. The geisha profession and the independent flower district system were only gradually established much later. In other words, Gion began with pilgrims, while the Ponto-cho area was shaped by water transport and merchants . Different geographical locations attracted different guests, leading tea houses, inns, and performances to gradually gather in these areas. I first walked into Pontocho over 20. years ago while scouting routes for a tour. Turning in from Shijo Street, the alley was very narrow, but the latticed doors and small signs were packed side by side; when the lights came on at dusk, it felt very different from the main street outside. Ever since then, whenever friends visit Kyoto for the first time, I love taking them through this stretch. It’s just really hard to film there; the alley is too narrow to pull the lens back, and it’s very crowded at night. So, one time I decided to come early in the morning, which allowed me to see those latticed tea house nameplates and the alley details much more clearly. After seeing. the streets by day, I went on to learn about the kind of people hosted here in the past. Pontocho is much more than just an atmospheric alley at night. Regarding Geiko and Maiko, there are distinctions to be made. Kyoto refers to mature professionals as "Geiko," while "Maiko" are in the apprentice stage, learning dance, singing, and traditional etiquette. Okiya provide them with a place to live and train, while tea houses arrange the banquet cuisine and the attendance of the Geiko . Some traditional tea houses do not accept unfamiliar guests, which is.

# 藝妓與舞妓有什麼不同

related to their method of arranging banquets based on long-term relationships and credit. For travelers , standing on the street seeing the latticed doors, nameplates, and lanterns is only seeing the exterior. Behind those doors lies a long-standing system of work and life. This explains why encountering a Geiko on the street doesn't mean meeting a performer ready for a photo—they are likely on their way to work. To appreciate Geiko, public dance performances and theater shows were later developed, allowing. general travelers more ease. Beyond the local residents and merchants. Kyoto also had people constantly arriving from afar. In the Edo period, the Tokaido connected Edo’s Nihonbashi to Kyoto’s Sanjo Ohashi Bridge. There were inns along the route, and travelers needed food and lodging, visited temples and shrines, and bought local souvenirs. Travel was restricted by social status, passage permits, and economic conditions, making it far less convenient than today. However, with the development of transportation and publishing, travel gradually became something more people aspired to. On the west side of Sanjo Ohashi Bridge,.

# 東海道旅人與老旅館的起點

there are bronze statues of Yajirobe and Kitahachi. They are travel companions from the book "Tokaidochu Hizakurige," who spent the journey gluttonously eating, misunderstanding dialects, and making fools of themselves through their own cleverness . The meaning of "Hizakurige" is to use your own feet as horses, traveling by walking. Since I started walking segments of the Tokaido road from Nihonbashi in Tokyo, seeing these two statues makes them feel even more familiar. Walking is tiring, you have to find places to eat and arrange accommodation, so novels from 200 years ago wrote about the troubles and humor. of travel, allowing readers who couldn't travel to journey along on paper. After travelers crossed the Sanjo Bridge, there were businesses nearby to cater to them. When people think of Tawaraya or Hiiragiya today, they mostly think of high-end ryokan, but their origins were related to serving travelers. Tawaraya started out as a business making straw hats, which attracted people on the road; Hiiragiya originally handled transportation and seafood, gradually shifting to become a hotelier. Therefore, from watching performances and shopping to buying local products and staying in inns,. many things travelers do in Kyoto today can actually be traced back to the Edo period. Kyoto's existing temples, shrines, imperial court, and entertainment districts, combined with relatively long-term peace and the constant flow of travelers, allowed this way of life to accumulate generation after generation. However, towards the end, Kyoto became the center of political conflict and war. When the Meiji Restoration arrived, the Emperor and the court gradually moved to Tokyo, leaving this city that had long hosted people from all over facing a crisis. With the court gone,.

# 幕末到明治，京都如何轉型

businesses and jobs that relied on it were affected, and the population and commerce declined for a time. If Kyoto was to continue developing, it needed new industries, education, and transportation, and it needed reasons for outsiders to visit. In 1869, with government promotion and resident funding, Kyoto established its first elementary schools, three years before the national school system was announced. Existing local self-governing organizations pooled their funds, and the schools even took on some local administrative, firefighting, and relief functions. When I visited the Kyoto City School History Museum, seeing the preserved desks, teaching materials, and school records gave me a concrete understanding of how much effort the city put into educating the next generation back then. Then, the Lake Biwa Canal brought water to Kyoto for transport and power generation, while railways and streetcars transformed how people moved about. These infrastructure projects allowed Kyoto to develop new industries and made it easier for people to arrive. However, the initiative most related to the aforementioned entertainment districts. was the hosting of expositions. In 1872 , in conjunction with the Kyoto Exposition, the Miyako Odori, performed by the Gion Kobu district, began, bringing the skills honed over years in the entertainment districts to a wider audience. Dances that once required an introduction to be seen at private banquets were now available to the public through ticketed performances, becoming a draw for out-of-town visitors. So, the Kyoto spring dance performances people might specifically plan to see today, while drawing on older memories, actually developed as public performance events during the.

# 博覽會與新京極，舞踊走向大眾

Meiji era. Traditions also find ways to adapt as new eras arrive. The " Shin-Kyogoku" district, opened in that same year, is another prime example. Kyoto opened this street on the east side of Shijo-dori, gathering theaters, playhouses, and eateries, with cinemas added later on. I used to just think of it as a busy place, but after a recent movie trip, I learned about the street's origins and realized it was developed as an entertainment district to draw crowds from the start. From the Shijo-Kawaramachi of the Edo period to. the Shin-Kyogoku of the Meiji era, the demand for theater and dining remained, though the performances, shops, and transport evolved—slowly shaping what we see today through Taisho era food, coffee, films, and new architecture. Kyoto. With this, history can turn into your next travel plan; let’s start with the Minamiza theater mentioned earlier—I’d photographed it from Shijo Bridge and walked past it countless times, but had never gone inside. It wasn't until I saw the movie.

# 把歷史排進行程：南座與花街表演

"National Treasure" that I suddenly wanted to sit in the theater, so I checked for the next day's show and bought a third-floor seat. I watched a Kamigata comedy that day, not Kabuki, but looking down at the red auditorium and the stage from the third floor, I still felt: "I've finally walked in." The theater building in front of me was largely completed in 1929, featuring a traditional "hafu" gable on the exterior, but the interior? It utilizes modern structural design, lighting, and stage equipment; its 400-year history has seen many building changes, yet it continues to welcome audiences. I later. had the opportunity to enter a Gion Kobu teahouse, watching geiko and maiko performances up close—some dancing, some playing the shamisen—and I finally understood the differences in their hairstyles, flowers, and outfits; the vague impressions from seeing them on the street turned into a concrete appreciation of their professional tradition. Private teahouse banquets require special arrangements, but public performances at Kaburenjo theaters are much easier to fit into a travel itinerary. I also once saw a limited-time performance in Pontocho that combined geiko dance, Japanese. opera, and Gion-matsuri themes; the content changes with each event, so check the schedule beforehand to find a show that interests you. Moving from the theater to daily life, the primary schools mentioned earlier are now accessible to travelers today. For example, the Kyoto International Manga Museum was formerly Tatsuike Primary School. Bookshelves line the old classrooms and hallways, where you can pick up a manga and sit down to read. You might have been stopped by a teacher for reading manga in class before, but now you can buy a ticket to.

# 舊小學校變成漫畫館與旅館

come in and read, while another school has become the Kyoto. Art Center; the corridors still retain a school-like feel, while the classrooms now host exhibitions, creative activities, and cafes. As for the former primary school by the Kamo River, I actually stayed there for a night. The guest rooms are modern hotel facilities. At night, the arches and long windows of the old school building lit up, reminding me of when I came to take photos years ago, back when it was still a closed school. Next to the school gate is a plaque marking the birthplace of Japanese cinema. This land once belonged to the. Kyoto Electric Light Company. In 1897, Seitaro Shibata brought back film projection equipment from France and held trials here. The school moved in later; I originally only meant to stay the night, but ended up encountering the beginnings of Kyoto's film history. If you are looking for a place to have coffee, the Kyoto Prefectural Office Old Main Building is also well worth a visit. Completed in 1904, its facade is symmetrical, with an entrance and grand staircase in the center. Walking inside , you can still see long corridors and exquisite woodwork. Interestingly, although it is called the "Old Main.

# 京都府廳舊本館與老咖啡店

Building," some rooms are still used as office space today. When I went there, aside from seeing the architecture, I also visited the ground-floor cafe, " Salon 1904." The name is taken from the year the building was completed, managed by Maeda Coffee, with white walls, dark wainscoting, and red carpets. There is also furniture that was used in government offices, which now allows guests to sit down and enjoy a coffee. One of the coffees is called "Shigemitsu," named after the building's designer, Matsumuro Shigemitsu. I had originally read his name on an information plaque, and upon. reaching the cafe, I unexpectedly encountered him again on the menu. After finishing a cup, the architect's name was at least much easier to remember. Kyoto's modern life has also left many stories in its old shops, such as Inoda Coffee. In 1940, it originally started as a coffee bean wholesaler, and only opened a cafe after the war in 1947. I once stayed nearby and walked into the main shop for breakfast in the morning. Behind the windowpane were western-style chairs and staff members in white uniforms. The era of war affected. materials and jobs, and also changed many families. Eventually, after the war, some people returned to Kyoto to reopen their shops. One that has a very deep connection with Taiwan is Gion Tsujiri. Walking from Hanamikoji to Shijo-dori, you may have seen their sign or eaten their matcha soft-serve, and the dessert shop upstairs is called Saryo Tsujiri. I originally thought the story of Uji tea should start in Uji, but later realized this shop must also pass through Taipei. The brand originated from a tea merchant in Uji,.

# 祇園辻利與台灣的淵源

Tsujiriemon. Later, Tokusaburo Miyoshi came to Taiwan in 1899 to run the " Tsujiri Tea Shop" in Taipei, where he also researched and promoted Taiwanese tea. He lived in Taiwan for many years, and the next generation of his family grew up there as well. After World War II, the Miyoshi family returned to Japan and reopened the store in Gion, Kyoto, in 1948. The Tokusaburo Miyoshi documents preserved at the Academia Sinica's Institute of Taiwan History also record the relationship between this Taipei tea shop and "Tsujiri." Therefore, behind this familiar Kyoto. brand today lies the journey of a family returning from Taiwan to Japan to rebuild their business. That time, I finally went up to the second floor of the main store and ordered the "Kyoto no Kiwami." The staff first brought cold-brewed tea, then a dessert with matcha ice cream, agar jelly, and shiratama; I just wanted to eat matcha, but ended up reading the history of Taipei from the shop's story. Finally, there is a pair of places that are hundreds of years apart, yet can be understood together. The aforementioned Emperor Go-Mizunoo, many years after his abdication, built the Shugakuin.

# 修學院離宮與京都迎賓館

Imperial Villa in the northeast of Kyoto in his later years. I followed the tour from the Lower Villa, passing through pine trees, paths, and ridges, until reaching the Rinyu-tei, where the Yokuryuchi pond unfolded below. It turns out that a royal villa can incorporate the surrounding rural fields and mountain scenery into the view for visitors. Later, I applied to visit the Kyoto State Guest House within the Kyoto Imperial Palace grounds, and encountered bridges, lacquerware, and plants again. However, this is a national facility that only. opened in 2005 to host foreign heads of state and important guests. Walking through the tour route, you see rooms used for meetings, banquets, and performances in sequence; the woodwork and lacquerware all have different craftsmanship, and I was deeply impressed by the long table in the main dining room. It is a 12-meter table; the black tabletop reflects the window light and looks very formal, but there is space underneath to hang your legs, allowing foreign guests unaccustomed to kneeling to dine more comfortably. I really like this detail, because. entertaining guests ultimately requires considering how they sit and how they will use the space. Four hundred years ago, the receptions held by the Emperor and the Shogun embodied the memories of Kyoto. Today, these crafts continue to be used in different buildings to meet modern needs. If you would like to visit the Kyoto State Guest House in person, you can plan your trip according to the public schedule released by the Cabinet Office. Therefore, much of today’s Kyoto experience for travelers begins in the Edo period. By understanding how it evolved through name changes, one can. better grasp what we see before us now. There are many more stories from this journey, which I have compiled in my newly released book, "Kyoto Times," so please feel free to continue reading if you are interested. Finally, I would like to ask you a few questions: First, have you ever seen a performance in Kyoto? Which one left the deepest impression on you? Second, do you prefer the Kyoto Imperial Palace or the Sento Imperial Palace? Third, which place would you most like to visit on your next trip to Kyoto? Fourth, if you had to pick one scene in Kyoto that seems traditional but actually appeared.

# 結語與留言互動

quite recently, which one would it be? Please leave a comment to let me know and share your thoughts with fellow viewers. Alright, that is all for this episode. Remember to like, subscribe, hit the notification bell, and join the channel membership to stay tuned for more history and travel topics from the "Kyoto Times" perspective. See you next time. Bye.

2026 年是寬永行幸四百年。這集從 1626 年德川將軍迎接後水尾天皇到二条城的五天出發，走訪阿國與歌舞伎、祇園與先斗町的花街、東海道的旅人、番組小學校、老咖啡店與辻利茶舖，看今天旅客熟悉的京都生活如何一步步形成。看完之後，南座、花街、舊小學校與京都府廳舊本館會連成一條線，下次到京都也更容易安排自己的行程。

item.description:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OdOfyIE0cpY

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入了解京都「寬永行幸」400週年背後，皇室與幕府如何透過盛事推動璀璨的寬永文化與工藝巔峰。
  • 探尋日本傳統「歌舞伎」從出雲阿國的前衛河原演出，一路演變至今日四條南座劇場的歷史脈絡。
  • 釐清祇園與先斗町等知名「花街」因參拜信仰與運河商貿而生的不同淵源，並認識藝妓與舞妓的文化制度。

摘要

寬永行幸：牽動江戶初期文化繁盛的世紀盛事

說書人工頭堅指出，2026年京都將迎來寬永行幸400週年紀念。回溯至1626年，退位將軍德川秀忠與三代將軍德川家光邀請後水尾天皇行幸二條城展開為期五天的盛會。彼時大坂之陣剛落幕不久，政治重心雖已轉移至江戶，但幕府藉由迎請兼具親屬關係的天皇，展現政權穩定並促進公武融和。二條城為此大幅擴建與彩繪裝飾，匯聚了頂尖畫師、詩人、樂師與工藝匠人，這場世紀盛會不僅展示了豐厚的文化底蘊，亦催生了後世所稱的寬永文化，而平民百姓在街道夾道觀看的身影，也悄然拉開了江戶市井娛樂生活蓬勃發展的序幕。

出雲阿國的創新舞步：歌舞伎與四條河原町的繁榮

與此同時，京都的民間娛樂亦迎來劃時代的變革。1603年德川家康就任征夷大將軍之際，出雲阿國在京都開創了前衛且略帶叛逆風格的舞作，成為現代歌舞伎的起源。阿國女扮男裝、身著華服進行逗趣演出，吸引大量觀眾駐足於神社與四條河原町的臨時舞台。隨著幕府後續頒令禁止女性與少年登台，歌舞伎逐漸演變成由成年男性專職扮演的傳統形式。四條一帶曾經林立的七座劇場，歷經火災與更迭後，如今僅存南座延續香火；而觀賞戲劇所帶動的餐飲、道具製作與住宿需求，更奠定了四條河原町繁盛的商業網絡。

水運與信仰交織：祇園、先斗町花街與藝妓文化

沿著劇場周邊蔓延的生活圈進一步孕育了京都獨特的花街文化。工頭堅分析，祇園最初是為八坂神社進香客提供茶水休息的「水茶屋」，因需求擴大而漸漸轉型為擁有幕府營業許可的花街；而先斗町則夾在鴨川與高瀨川之間，依托著高瀨川的水運樞紐聚集舟船工與各地客商，進而發展出茶屋、旅社與藝能空間。兩地因地理與客群不同而展現相異風貌，並確立了由成年的藝妓與見習階段的舞妓組成的傳承體系，茶屋更依循「不接生客」的信用制度維持宴席品質，使江戶時代的生活風貌在今日京都窄巷間依然歷久彌新。

================================================

# 寬永行幸四百年，京都從哪裡來

Hello everyone, I’m your travel guide , Gong Tou-Jian. On December 6, 2026, Kyoto plans to reenact the procession of the Emperor traveling to Nijo Castle 400 years ago. Why would a journey that lasted only five days back then be commemorated so solemnly 400 years later? How did the familiar Kabuki theaters, Hanamachi districts, teahouses, and ryokan we visit in Kyoto today gradually take shape? My sequel to the widely loved "Kyoto Time," titled "Gong Tou-Jian’s Kyoto Time II : Modern Era," has also just been released. As I continue to visit Kyoto,. I increasingly feel that much of the life experienced by today's travelers must be traced back to the Edo period. In this episode, we’ll look at the " 400th Anniversary of the Kan'ei Imperial Visit" to see how the people of Kyoto back then enjoyed theater, conducted business, and entertained guests, leading to the places where we can now buy tickets for performances, grab a coffee, or even stay overnight. If you enjoy this content, you are welcome to join the channel membership and walk further along this path with me. So, let’s...First of all...The. term "Gyoko" refers to an imperial visit. In 1626, the retired Shogun Tokugawa Hidetada and the third Shogun, Tokugawa Iemitsu, jointly welcomed Emperor Go-Mizunoo to Nijo Castle for a five-day stay. It had been only 11 years since the Siege of Osaka and the fall of the Toyotomi clan. The center of Japanese political operations had already shifted to Edo, but the Emperor and the Imperial Court remained in Kyoto, with Nijo Castle serving as the Shogun’s residence during his visits. The Shogun invited the Emperor to foster harmony, bringing feudal lords from across the country together to.

# 寬永行幸：將軍迎接天皇的五天

showcase the stability growing under Tokugawa rule through this grand event. There was also a family connection: the Emperor’s consort, Tokugawa Masako, was Hidetada’s daughter and Iemitsu’s sister, who later became known as Tofukumon-in. In other words, the people welcoming the Emperor were simultaneously his father-in-law and his brother-in-law. Of course, the power dynamic between the Court and the Shogunate did not mean that becoming in-laws ended all conflict. However, this time, let’s put the politics in the background and look at what Kyoto prepared for those five days. To host. the Emperor, the Shogunate expanded the castle, renovated the palaces and gardens, commissioned artists to paint wall murals, and arranged banquets, court music, Noh plays, and other cultural activities. Beyond painters, poets, and musicians, it was also necessary to prepare exquisite cuisine and various gifts. I have introduced the architecture of Nijo Castle before, so I won't go into detail here, but these preparations perfectly demonstrate just how much craftsmanship was gathered in Kyoto at that time. Emperor Go-Mizunoo himself loved poetry , tea, and flower arranging. Interactions between the imperial court. , nobility, temples, the samurai class, and wealthy merchants provided opportunities for painting, gardening, and crafts to flourish. The later " Kanei Culture" can be understood within this context, and this procession was a grand display of the cultural activities of the time. Interestingly, the "Nijo Castle Procession" screen painting depicts not only the procession itself but also the crowds watching along the route. While the Emperor and the Shogun were the stars of the ceremony, many ordinary people were also on the streets, leaving behind details of their lives in how. they dressed and watched the event. This autumn, the Sen-oku Hakuko Kan and The Museum of Kyoto are holding related exhibitions, while in December, the procession itself will be reenacted— these are two separate events. Thinking beyond the crowds in the screen painting, there are more stories of Kyoto life outside the court. For this, we must shift our focus back three years to the very beginning of the Edo period. In 1603, the same year Tokugawa Ieyasu was appointed Shogun, another.

# 阿國銅像與歌舞伎的起點

event with significant later influence took place in Kyoto: the performances of Izumo no Okuni began. Walking out from Shijo Station, near the Shijo Bridge, you can see a bronze statue of a woman. With a fan in one hand and a long sword slung behind her shoulder, her striking pose is that of Okuni. Many travelers pass by her on their way to the Minami-za theater, Hanamikoji, or the shrines. There is much uncertainty surrounding Okuni's life, but the performances she introduced are now considered the origins of Kabuki. Back then, the term "kabuki" carried a connotation of deviating from the norm and deliberately striking a different pose. She would dress as a man in flamboyant costumes, performing themes such as tea house entertainment and comedic roles, attracting large crowds to watch. When we think of Kabuki today , we might imagine formal theaters, traditional costumes, and actors from hereditary lineages, but in Okuni’s time, it was a form of entertainment that was even considered a bit daring. Many performances later labeled as " traditional" first drew attention precisely because they differed from. existing forms. However, the presence of a bronze statue by the bridge does not necessarily mean that Okuni’s first performance took place right at the foot of that statue. The "Okuni Kabuki" screen painting, held by the Kyoto National Museum, depicts her performing on a Noh stage at the Kitano Tenmangu Shrine. Performances at the time were likely held at shrines or on temporary stages in riverbeds, rather than in fixed, dedicated theater buildings. As the trend caught on and more groups began to imitate her, the Shijo riverbed grew increasingly lively . Later, the shogunate banned performances by women and youths, so.

actors became primarily adult males, and female roles were played by men, gradually developing the form we are familiar with today. In the Shijo-Kawaramachi area, there were seven authorized theaters during the early Edo period. Their names and locations shifted due to fires, renovations, and management changes, eventually leaving only the Minami-za and Kita-za. By the Meiji era, the Kita-za also closed, leaving only the Minami-za to continue performances today. If you walk over there, the name of the Kita-za still remains on the storefronts near Shijo Bridge, while. the Minami-za continues to hang its performance banners across Shijo-dori. Buying souvenirs, watching plays, and dining—the activities concentrated in this area today all have their own unique histories when you look back. Back then, for a theater to operate, the surrounding area needed places to eat and places for workers to rest. Actors required costumes, makeup, and props, and audiences would also look for places to dine after the show; the performances drew people, and the people brought business. Kyoto's entertainment life flourished amidst this constant flow. So. From here, one. can walk to the nearby hanamachi ( geisha districts). Although Kabuki actors, geiko, and maiko often appear together in the impressions foreign tourists have of Kyoto, their work and history are actually quite different. Kabuki is performed in theaters, while Kyoto’s geiko and maiko entertain guests at banquets with dance, music, and conversation. While there is a history of exchange between them, the hanamachi have their own distinct development process. The origins of the Gion district are linked to the area in front of today's Yasaka Shrine. Pilgrims needed tea and rest, leading.

# 祇園與先斗町，花街怎麼形成

to the creation of "water tea houses," which gradually began to offer more services as the number of guests and their needs grew. By the mid-Edo period , some tea houses obtained operating permits from the shogunate, and the hanamachi system we are familiar with today was gradually formed through these changes. As for the Ponto-cho area on the other side, it must be understood through its waterways. It is nestled between the Kamo River and the Takase River; the Takase River was used for transporting goods, attracting boatmen, merchants, and travelers to the vicinity. After the western bank of. the river was reclaimed, there was land available for development. Around 1712, tea houses and inns—places for socializing and lodging—began to appear. The geisha profession and the independent flower district system were only gradually established much later. In other words, Gion began with pilgrims, while the Ponto-cho area was shaped by water transport and merchants . Different geographical locations attracted different guests, leading tea houses, inns, and performances to gradually gather in these areas. I first walked into Pontocho over 20. years ago while scouting routes for a tour. Turning in from Shijo Street, the alley was very narrow, but the latticed doors and small signs were packed side by side; when the lights came on at dusk, it felt very different from the main street outside. Ever since then, whenever friends visit Kyoto for the first time, I love taking them through this stretch. It’s just really hard to film there; the alley is too narrow to pull the lens back, and it’s very crowded at night. So, one time I decided to come early in the morning, which allowed me to see those latticed tea house nameplates and the alley details much more clearly. After seeing. the streets by day, I went on to learn about the kind of people hosted here in the past. Pontocho is much more than just an atmospheric alley at night. Regarding Geiko and Maiko, there are distinctions to be made. Kyoto refers to mature professionals as "Geiko," while "Maiko" are in the apprentice stage, learning dance, singing, and traditional etiquette. Okiya provide them with a place to live and train, while tea houses arrange the banquet cuisine and the attendance of the Geiko . Some traditional tea houses do not accept unfamiliar guests, which is.

# 藝妓與舞妓有什麼不同

related to their method of arranging banquets based on long-term relationships and credit. For travelers , standing on the street seeing the latticed doors, nameplates, and lanterns is only seeing the exterior. Behind those doors lies a long-standing system of work and life. This explains why encountering a Geiko on the street doesn't mean meeting a performer ready for a photo—they are likely on their way to work. To appreciate Geiko, public dance performances and theater shows were later developed, allowing. general travelers more ease. Beyond the local residents and merchants. Kyoto also had people constantly arriving from afar. In the Edo period, the Tokaido connected Edo’s Nihonbashi to Kyoto’s Sanjo Ohashi Bridge. There were inns along the route, and travelers needed food and lodging, visited temples and shrines, and bought local souvenirs. Travel was restricted by social status, passage permits, and economic conditions, making it far less convenient than today. However, with the development of transportation and publishing, travel gradually became something more people aspired to. On the west side of Sanjo Ohashi Bridge,.

# 東海道旅人與老旅館的起點

there are bronze statues of Yajirobe and Kitahachi. They are travel companions from the book "Tokaidochu Hizakurige," who spent the journey gluttonously eating, misunderstanding dialects, and making fools of themselves through their own cleverness . The meaning of "Hizakurige" is to use your own feet as horses, traveling by walking. Since I started walking segments of the Tokaido road from Nihonbashi in Tokyo, seeing these two statues makes them feel even more familiar. Walking is tiring, you have to find places to eat and arrange accommodation, so novels from 200 years ago wrote about the troubles and humor. of travel, allowing readers who couldn't travel to journey along on paper. After travelers crossed the Sanjo Bridge, there were businesses nearby to cater to them. When people think of Tawaraya or Hiiragiya today, they mostly think of high-end ryokan, but their origins were related to serving travelers. Tawaraya started out as a business making straw hats, which attracted people on the road; Hiiragiya originally handled transportation and seafood, gradually shifting to become a hotelier. Therefore, from watching performances and shopping to buying local products and staying in inns,. many things travelers do in Kyoto today can actually be traced back to the Edo period. Kyoto's existing temples, shrines, imperial court, and entertainment districts, combined with relatively long-term peace and the constant flow of travelers, allowed this way of life to accumulate generation after generation. However, towards the end, Kyoto became the center of political conflict and war. When the Meiji Restoration arrived, the Emperor and the court gradually moved to Tokyo, leaving this city that had long hosted people from all over facing a crisis. With the court gone,.

# 幕末到明治，京都如何轉型

businesses and jobs that relied on it were affected, and the population and commerce declined for a time. If Kyoto was to continue developing, it needed new industries, education, and transportation, and it needed reasons for outsiders to visit. In 1869, with government promotion and resident funding, Kyoto established its first elementary schools, three years before the national school system was announced. Existing local self-governing organizations pooled their funds, and the schools even took on some local administrative, firefighting, and relief functions. When I visited the Kyoto City School History Museum, seeing the preserved desks, teaching materials, and school records gave me a concrete understanding of how much effort the city put into educating the next generation back then. Then, the Lake Biwa Canal brought water to Kyoto for transport and power generation, while railways and streetcars transformed how people moved about. These infrastructure projects allowed Kyoto to develop new industries and made it easier for people to arrive. However, the initiative most related to the aforementioned entertainment districts. was the hosting of expositions. In 1872 , in conjunction with the Kyoto Exposition, the Miyako Odori, performed by the Gion Kobu district, began, bringing the skills honed over years in the entertainment districts to a wider audience. Dances that once required an introduction to be seen at private banquets were now available to the public through ticketed performances, becoming a draw for out-of-town visitors. So, the Kyoto spring dance performances people might specifically plan to see today, while drawing on older memories, actually developed as public performance events during the.

# 博覽會與新京極，舞踊走向大眾

Meiji era. Traditions also find ways to adapt as new eras arrive. The " Shin-Kyogoku" district, opened in that same year, is another prime example. Kyoto opened this street on the east side of Shijo-dori, gathering theaters, playhouses, and eateries, with cinemas added later on. I used to just think of it as a busy place, but after a recent movie trip, I learned about the street's origins and realized it was developed as an entertainment district to draw crowds from the start. From the Shijo-Kawaramachi of the Edo period to. the Shin-Kyogoku of the Meiji era, the demand for theater and dining remained, though the performances, shops, and transport evolved—slowly shaping what we see today through Taisho era food, coffee, films, and new architecture. Kyoto. With this, history can turn into your next travel plan; let’s start with the Minamiza theater mentioned earlier—I’d photographed it from Shijo Bridge and walked past it countless times, but had never gone inside. It wasn't until I saw the movie.

# 把歷史排進行程：南座與花街表演

"National Treasure" that I suddenly wanted to sit in the theater, so I checked for the next day's show and bought a third-floor seat. I watched a Kamigata comedy that day, not Kabuki, but looking down at the red auditorium and the stage from the third floor, I still felt: "I've finally walked in." The theater building in front of me was largely completed in 1929, featuring a traditional "hafu" gable on the exterior, but the interior? It utilizes modern structural design, lighting, and stage equipment; its 400-year history has seen many building changes, yet it continues to welcome audiences. I later. had the opportunity to enter a Gion Kobu teahouse, watching geiko and maiko performances up close—some dancing, some playing the shamisen—and I finally understood the differences in their hairstyles, flowers, and outfits; the vague impressions from seeing them on the street turned into a concrete appreciation of their professional tradition. Private teahouse banquets require special arrangements, but public performances at Kaburenjo theaters are much easier to fit into a travel itinerary. I also once saw a limited-time performance in Pontocho that combined geiko dance, Japanese. opera, and Gion-matsuri themes; the content changes with each event, so check the schedule beforehand to find a show that interests you. Moving from the theater to daily life, the primary schools mentioned earlier are now accessible to travelers today. For example, the Kyoto International Manga Museum was formerly Tatsuike Primary School. Bookshelves line the old classrooms and hallways, where you can pick up a manga and sit down to read. You might have been stopped by a teacher for reading manga in class before, but now you can buy a ticket to.

# 舊小學校變成漫畫館與旅館

come in and read, while another school has become the Kyoto. Art Center; the corridors still retain a school-like feel, while the classrooms now host exhibitions, creative activities, and cafes. As for the former primary school by the Kamo River, I actually stayed there for a night. The guest rooms are modern hotel facilities. At night, the arches and long windows of the old school building lit up, reminding me of when I came to take photos years ago, back when it was still a closed school. Next to the school gate is a plaque marking the birthplace of Japanese cinema. This land once belonged to the. Kyoto Electric Light Company. In 1897, Seitaro Shibata brought back film projection equipment from France and held trials here. The school moved in later; I originally only meant to stay the night, but ended up encountering the beginnings of Kyoto's film history. If you are looking for a place to have coffee, the Kyoto Prefectural Office Old Main Building is also well worth a visit. Completed in 1904, its facade is symmetrical, with an entrance and grand staircase in the center. Walking inside , you can still see long corridors and exquisite woodwork. Interestingly, although it is called the "Old Main.

# 京都府廳舊本館與老咖啡店

Building," some rooms are still used as office space today. When I went there, aside from seeing the architecture, I also visited the ground-floor cafe, " Salon 1904." The name is taken from the year the building was completed, managed by Maeda Coffee, with white walls, dark wainscoting, and red carpets. There is also furniture that was used in government offices, which now allows guests to sit down and enjoy a coffee. One of the coffees is called "Shigemitsu," named after the building's designer, Matsumuro Shigemitsu. I had originally read his name on an information plaque, and upon. reaching the cafe, I unexpectedly encountered him again on the menu. After finishing a cup, the architect's name was at least much easier to remember. Kyoto's modern life has also left many stories in its old shops, such as Inoda Coffee. In 1940, it originally started as a coffee bean wholesaler, and only opened a cafe after the war in 1947. I once stayed nearby and walked into the main shop for breakfast in the morning. Behind the windowpane were western-style chairs and staff members in white uniforms. The era of war affected. materials and jobs, and also changed many families. Eventually, after the war, some people returned to Kyoto to reopen their shops. One that has a very deep connection with Taiwan is Gion Tsujiri. Walking from Hanamikoji to Shijo-dori, you may have seen their sign or eaten their matcha soft-serve, and the dessert shop upstairs is called Saryo Tsujiri. I originally thought the story of Uji tea should start in Uji, but later realized this shop must also pass through Taipei. The brand originated from a tea merchant in Uji,.

# 祇園辻利與台灣的淵源

Tsujiriemon. Later, Tokusaburo Miyoshi came to Taiwan in 1899 to run the " Tsujiri Tea Shop" in Taipei, where he also researched and promoted Taiwanese tea. He lived in Taiwan for many years, and the next generation of his family grew up there as well. After World War II, the Miyoshi family returned to Japan and reopened the store in Gion, Kyoto, in 1948. The Tokusaburo Miyoshi documents preserved at the Academia Sinica's Institute of Taiwan History also record the relationship between this Taipei tea shop and "Tsujiri." Therefore, behind this familiar Kyoto. brand today lies the journey of a family returning from Taiwan to Japan to rebuild their business. That time, I finally went up to the second floor of the main store and ordered the "Kyoto no Kiwami." The staff first brought cold-brewed tea, then a dessert with matcha ice cream, agar jelly, and shiratama; I just wanted to eat matcha, but ended up reading the history of Taipei from the shop's story. Finally, there is a pair of places that are hundreds of years apart, yet can be understood together. The aforementioned Emperor Go-Mizunoo, many years after his abdication, built the Shugakuin.

# 修學院離宮與京都迎賓館

Imperial Villa in the northeast of Kyoto in his later years. I followed the tour from the Lower Villa, passing through pine trees, paths, and ridges, until reaching the Rinyu-tei, where the Yokuryuchi pond unfolded below. It turns out that a royal villa can incorporate the surrounding rural fields and mountain scenery into the view for visitors. Later, I applied to visit the Kyoto State Guest House within the Kyoto Imperial Palace grounds, and encountered bridges, lacquerware, and plants again. However, this is a national facility that only. opened in 2005 to host foreign heads of state and important guests. Walking through the tour route, you see rooms used for meetings, banquets, and performances in sequence; the woodwork and lacquerware all have different craftsmanship, and I was deeply impressed by the long table in the main dining room. It is a 12-meter table; the black tabletop reflects the window light and looks very formal, but there is space underneath to hang your legs, allowing foreign guests unaccustomed to kneeling to dine more comfortably. I really like this detail, because. entertaining guests ultimately requires considering how they sit and how they will use the space. Four hundred years ago, the receptions held by the Emperor and the Shogun embodied the memories of Kyoto. Today, these crafts continue to be used in different buildings to meet modern needs. If you would like to visit the Kyoto State Guest House in person, you can plan your trip according to the public schedule released by the Cabinet Office. Therefore, much of today’s Kyoto experience for travelers begins in the Edo period. By understanding how it evolved through name changes, one can. better grasp what we see before us now. There are many more stories from this journey, which I have compiled in my newly released book, "Kyoto Times," so please feel free to continue reading if you are interested. Finally, I would like to ask you a few questions: First, have you ever seen a performance in Kyoto? Which one left the deepest impression on you? Second, do you prefer the Kyoto Imperial Palace or the Sento Imperial Palace? Third, which place would you most like to visit on your next trip to Kyoto? Fourth, if you had to pick one scene in Kyoto that seems traditional but actually appeared.

# 結語與留言互動

quite recently, which one would it be? Please leave a comment to let me know and share your thoughts with fellow viewers. Alright, that is all for this episode. Remember to like, subscribe, hit the notification bell, and join the channel membership to stay tuned for more history and travel topics from the "Kyoto Times" perspective. See you next time. Bye.

=============

從四百年前的寬永行幸出發，看京都的歌舞伎、花街、老舖與旅館怎麼一路走到今天。

2026 年是寬永行幸四百年。這集從 1626 年德川將軍迎接後水尾天皇到二条城的五天出發，走訪阿國與歌舞伎、祇園與先斗町的花街、東海道的旅人、番組小學校、老咖啡店與辻利茶舖，看今天旅客熟悉的京都生活如何一步步形成。看完之後，南座、花街、舊小學校與京都府廳舊本館會連成一條線，下次到京都也更容易安排自己的行程。

成為這個頻道的會員並獲得福利：

item.content:encoded:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OdOfyIE0cpY

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入了解京都「寬永行幸」400週年背後，皇室與幕府如何透過盛事推動璀璨的寬永文化與工藝巔峰。
  • 探尋日本傳統「歌舞伎」從出雲阿國的前衛河原演出，一路演變至今日四條南座劇場的歷史脈絡。
  • 釐清祇園與先斗町等知名「花街」因參拜信仰與運河商貿而生的不同淵源，並認識藝妓與舞妓的文化制度。

摘要

寬永行幸：牽動江戶初期文化繁盛的世紀盛事

說書人工頭堅指出，2026年京都將迎來寬永行幸400週年紀念。回溯至1626年，退位將軍德川秀忠與三代將軍德川家光邀請後水尾天皇行幸二條城展開為期五天的盛會。彼時大坂之陣剛落幕不久，政治重心雖已轉移至江戶，但幕府藉由迎請兼具親屬關係的天皇，展現政權穩定並促進公武融和。二條城為此大幅擴建與彩繪裝飾，匯聚了頂尖畫師、詩人、樂師與工藝匠人，這場世紀盛會不僅展示了豐厚的文化底蘊，亦催生了後世所稱的寬永文化，而平民百姓在街道夾道觀看的身影，也悄然拉開了江戶市井娛樂生活蓬勃發展的序幕。

出雲阿國的創新舞步：歌舞伎與四條河原町的繁榮

與此同時，京都的民間娛樂亦迎來劃時代的變革。1603年德川家康就任征夷大將軍之際，出雲阿國在京都開創了前衛且略帶叛逆風格的舞作，成為現代歌舞伎的起源。阿國女扮男裝、身著華服進行逗趣演出，吸引大量觀眾駐足於神社與四條河原町的臨時舞台。隨著幕府後續頒令禁止女性與少年登台，歌舞伎逐漸演變成由成年男性專職扮演的傳統形式。四條一帶曾經林立的七座劇場，歷經火災與更迭後，如今僅存南座延續香火；而觀賞戲劇所帶動的餐飲、道具製作與住宿需求，更奠定了四條河原町繁盛的商業網絡。

水運與信仰交織：祇園、先斗町花街與藝妓文化

沿著劇場周邊蔓延的生活圈進一步孕育了京都獨特的花街文化。工頭堅分析，祇園最初是為八坂神社進香客提供茶水休息的「水茶屋」，因需求擴大而漸漸轉型為擁有幕府營業許可的花街；而先斗町則夾在鴨川與高瀨川之間，依托著高瀨川的水運樞紐聚集舟船工與各地客商，進而發展出茶屋、旅社與藝能空間。兩地因地理與客群不同而展現相異風貌，並確立了由成年的藝妓與見習階段的舞妓組成的傳承體系，茶屋更依循「不接生客」的信用制度維持宴席品質，使江戶時代的生活風貌在今日京都窄巷間依然歷久彌新。

================================================

# 寬永行幸四百年，京都從哪裡來

Hello everyone, I’m your travel guide , Gong Tou-Jian. On December 6, 2026, Kyoto plans to reenact the procession of the Emperor traveling to Nijo Castle 400 years ago. Why would a journey that lasted only five days back then be commemorated so solemnly 400 years later? How did the familiar Kabuki theaters, Hanamachi districts, teahouses, and ryokan we visit in Kyoto today gradually take shape? My sequel to the widely loved "Kyoto Time," titled "Gong Tou-Jian’s Kyoto Time II : Modern Era," has also just been released. As I continue to visit Kyoto,. I increasingly feel that much of the life experienced by today's travelers must be traced back to the Edo period. In this episode, we’ll look at the " 400th Anniversary of the Kan'ei Imperial Visit" to see how the people of Kyoto back then enjoyed theater, conducted business, and entertained guests, leading to the places where we can now buy tickets for performances, grab a coffee, or even stay overnight. If you enjoy this content, you are welcome to join the channel membership and walk further along this path with me. So, let’s...First of all...The. term "Gyoko" refers to an imperial visit. In 1626, the retired Shogun Tokugawa Hidetada and the third Shogun, Tokugawa Iemitsu, jointly welcomed Emperor Go-Mizunoo to Nijo Castle for a five-day stay. It had been only 11 years since the Siege of Osaka and the fall of the Toyotomi clan. The center of Japanese political operations had already shifted to Edo, but the Emperor and the Imperial Court remained in Kyoto, with Nijo Castle serving as the Shogun’s residence during his visits. The Shogun invited the Emperor to foster harmony, bringing feudal lords from across the country together to.

# 寬永行幸：將軍迎接天皇的五天

showcase the stability growing under Tokugawa rule through this grand event. There was also a family connection: the Emperor’s consort, Tokugawa Masako, was Hidetada’s daughter and Iemitsu’s sister, who later became known as Tofukumon-in. In other words, the people welcoming the Emperor were simultaneously his father-in-law and his brother-in-law. Of course, the power dynamic between the Court and the Shogunate did not mean that becoming in-laws ended all conflict. However, this time, let’s put the politics in the background and look at what Kyoto prepared for those five days. To host. the Emperor, the Shogunate expanded the castle, renovated the palaces and gardens, commissioned artists to paint wall murals, and arranged banquets, court music, Noh plays, and other cultural activities. Beyond painters, poets, and musicians, it was also necessary to prepare exquisite cuisine and various gifts. I have introduced the architecture of Nijo Castle before, so I won't go into detail here, but these preparations perfectly demonstrate just how much craftsmanship was gathered in Kyoto at that time. Emperor Go-Mizunoo himself loved poetry , tea, and flower arranging. Interactions between the imperial court. , nobility, temples, the samurai class, and wealthy merchants provided opportunities for painting, gardening, and crafts to flourish. The later " Kanei Culture" can be understood within this context, and this procession was a grand display of the cultural activities of the time. Interestingly, the "Nijo Castle Procession" screen painting depicts not only the procession itself but also the crowds watching along the route. While the Emperor and the Shogun were the stars of the ceremony, many ordinary people were also on the streets, leaving behind details of their lives in how. they dressed and watched the event. This autumn, the Sen-oku Hakuko Kan and The Museum of Kyoto are holding related exhibitions, while in December, the procession itself will be reenacted— these are two separate events. Thinking beyond the crowds in the screen painting, there are more stories of Kyoto life outside the court. For this, we must shift our focus back three years to the very beginning of the Edo period. In 1603, the same year Tokugawa Ieyasu was appointed Shogun, another.

# 阿國銅像與歌舞伎的起點

event with significant later influence took place in Kyoto: the performances of Izumo no Okuni began. Walking out from Shijo Station, near the Shijo Bridge, you can see a bronze statue of a woman. With a fan in one hand and a long sword slung behind her shoulder, her striking pose is that of Okuni. Many travelers pass by her on their way to the Minami-za theater, Hanamikoji, or the shrines. There is much uncertainty surrounding Okuni's life, but the performances she introduced are now considered the origins of Kabuki. Back then, the term "kabuki" carried a connotation of deviating from the norm and deliberately striking a different pose. She would dress as a man in flamboyant costumes, performing themes such as tea house entertainment and comedic roles, attracting large crowds to watch. When we think of Kabuki today , we might imagine formal theaters, traditional costumes, and actors from hereditary lineages, but in Okuni’s time, it was a form of entertainment that was even considered a bit daring. Many performances later labeled as " traditional" first drew attention precisely because they differed from. existing forms. However, the presence of a bronze statue by the bridge does not necessarily mean that Okuni’s first performance took place right at the foot of that statue. The "Okuni Kabuki" screen painting, held by the Kyoto National Museum, depicts her performing on a Noh stage at the Kitano Tenmangu Shrine. Performances at the time were likely held at shrines or on temporary stages in riverbeds, rather than in fixed, dedicated theater buildings. As the trend caught on and more groups began to imitate her, the Shijo riverbed grew increasingly lively . Later, the shogunate banned performances by women and youths, so.

actors became primarily adult males, and female roles were played by men, gradually developing the form we are familiar with today. In the Shijo-Kawaramachi area, there were seven authorized theaters during the early Edo period. Their names and locations shifted due to fires, renovations, and management changes, eventually leaving only the Minami-za and Kita-za. By the Meiji era, the Kita-za also closed, leaving only the Minami-za to continue performances today. If you walk over there, the name of the Kita-za still remains on the storefronts near Shijo Bridge, while. the Minami-za continues to hang its performance banners across Shijo-dori. Buying souvenirs, watching plays, and dining—the activities concentrated in this area today all have their own unique histories when you look back. Back then, for a theater to operate, the surrounding area needed places to eat and places for workers to rest. Actors required costumes, makeup, and props, and audiences would also look for places to dine after the show; the performances drew people, and the people brought business. Kyoto's entertainment life flourished amidst this constant flow. So. From here, one. can walk to the nearby hanamachi ( geisha districts). Although Kabuki actors, geiko, and maiko often appear together in the impressions foreign tourists have of Kyoto, their work and history are actually quite different. Kabuki is performed in theaters, while Kyoto’s geiko and maiko entertain guests at banquets with dance, music, and conversation. While there is a history of exchange between them, the hanamachi have their own distinct development process. The origins of the Gion district are linked to the area in front of today's Yasaka Shrine. Pilgrims needed tea and rest, leading.

# 祇園與先斗町，花街怎麼形成

to the creation of "water tea houses," which gradually began to offer more services as the number of guests and their needs grew. By the mid-Edo period , some tea houses obtained operating permits from the shogunate, and the hanamachi system we are familiar with today was gradually formed through these changes. As for the Ponto-cho area on the other side, it must be understood through its waterways. It is nestled between the Kamo River and the Takase River; the Takase River was used for transporting goods, attracting boatmen, merchants, and travelers to the vicinity. After the western bank of. the river was reclaimed, there was land available for development. Around 1712, tea houses and inns—places for socializing and lodging—began to appear. The geisha profession and the independent flower district system were only gradually established much later. In other words, Gion began with pilgrims, while the Ponto-cho area was shaped by water transport and merchants . Different geographical locations attracted different guests, leading tea houses, inns, and performances to gradually gather in these areas. I first walked into Pontocho over 20. years ago while scouting routes for a tour. Turning in from Shijo Street, the alley was very narrow, but the latticed doors and small signs were packed side by side; when the lights came on at dusk, it felt very different from the main street outside. Ever since then, whenever friends visit Kyoto for the first time, I love taking them through this stretch. It’s just really hard to film there; the alley is too narrow to pull the lens back, and it’s very crowded at night. So, one time I decided to come early in the morning, which allowed me to see those latticed tea house nameplates and the alley details much more clearly. After seeing. the streets by day, I went on to learn about the kind of people hosted here in the past. Pontocho is much more than just an atmospheric alley at night. Regarding Geiko and Maiko, there are distinctions to be made. Kyoto refers to mature professionals as "Geiko," while "Maiko" are in the apprentice stage, learning dance, singing, and traditional etiquette. Okiya provide them with a place to live and train, while tea houses arrange the banquet cuisine and the attendance of the Geiko . Some traditional tea houses do not accept unfamiliar guests, which is.

# 藝妓與舞妓有什麼不同

related to their method of arranging banquets based on long-term relationships and credit. For travelers , standing on the street seeing the latticed doors, nameplates, and lanterns is only seeing the exterior. Behind those doors lies a long-standing system of work and life. This explains why encountering a Geiko on the street doesn't mean meeting a performer ready for a photo—they are likely on their way to work. To appreciate Geiko, public dance performances and theater shows were later developed, allowing. general travelers more ease. Beyond the local residents and merchants. Kyoto also had people constantly arriving from afar. In the Edo period, the Tokaido connected Edo’s Nihonbashi to Kyoto’s Sanjo Ohashi Bridge. There were inns along the route, and travelers needed food and lodging, visited temples and shrines, and bought local souvenirs. Travel was restricted by social status, passage permits, and economic conditions, making it far less convenient than today. However, with the development of transportation and publishing, travel gradually became something more people aspired to. On the west side of Sanjo Ohashi Bridge,.

# 東海道旅人與老旅館的起點

there are bronze statues of Yajirobe and Kitahachi. They are travel companions from the book "Tokaidochu Hizakurige," who spent the journey gluttonously eating, misunderstanding dialects, and making fools of themselves through their own cleverness . The meaning of "Hizakurige" is to use your own feet as horses, traveling by walking. Since I started walking segments of the Tokaido road from Nihonbashi in Tokyo, seeing these two statues makes them feel even more familiar. Walking is tiring, you have to find places to eat and arrange accommodation, so novels from 200 years ago wrote about the troubles and humor. of travel, allowing readers who couldn't travel to journey along on paper. After travelers crossed the Sanjo Bridge, there were businesses nearby to cater to them. When people think of Tawaraya or Hiiragiya today, they mostly think of high-end ryokan, but their origins were related to serving travelers. Tawaraya started out as a business making straw hats, which attracted people on the road; Hiiragiya originally handled transportation and seafood, gradually shifting to become a hotelier. Therefore, from watching performances and shopping to buying local products and staying in inns,. many things travelers do in Kyoto today can actually be traced back to the Edo period. Kyoto's existing temples, shrines, imperial court, and entertainment districts, combined with relatively long-term peace and the constant flow of travelers, allowed this way of life to accumulate generation after generation. However, towards the end, Kyoto became the center of political conflict and war. When the Meiji Restoration arrived, the Emperor and the court gradually moved to Tokyo, leaving this city that had long hosted people from all over facing a crisis. With the court gone,.

# 幕末到明治，京都如何轉型

businesses and jobs that relied on it were affected, and the population and commerce declined for a time. If Kyoto was to continue developing, it needed new industries, education, and transportation, and it needed reasons for outsiders to visit. In 1869, with government promotion and resident funding, Kyoto established its first elementary schools, three years before the national school system was announced. Existing local self-governing organizations pooled their funds, and the schools even took on some local administrative, firefighting, and relief functions. When I visited the Kyoto City School History Museum, seeing the preserved desks, teaching materials, and school records gave me a concrete understanding of how much effort the city put into educating the next generation back then. Then, the Lake Biwa Canal brought water to Kyoto for transport and power generation, while railways and streetcars transformed how people moved about. These infrastructure projects allowed Kyoto to develop new industries and made it easier for people to arrive. However, the initiative most related to the aforementioned entertainment districts. was the hosting of expositions. In 1872 , in conjunction with the Kyoto Exposition, the Miyako Odori, performed by the Gion Kobu district, began, bringing the skills honed over years in the entertainment districts to a wider audience. Dances that once required an introduction to be seen at private banquets were now available to the public through ticketed performances, becoming a draw for out-of-town visitors. So, the Kyoto spring dance performances people might specifically plan to see today, while drawing on older memories, actually developed as public performance events during the.

# 博覽會與新京極，舞踊走向大眾

Meiji era. Traditions also find ways to adapt as new eras arrive. The " Shin-Kyogoku" district, opened in that same year, is another prime example. Kyoto opened this street on the east side of Shijo-dori, gathering theaters, playhouses, and eateries, with cinemas added later on. I used to just think of it as a busy place, but after a recent movie trip, I learned about the street's origins and realized it was developed as an entertainment district to draw crowds from the start. From the Shijo-Kawaramachi of the Edo period to. the Shin-Kyogoku of the Meiji era, the demand for theater and dining remained, though the performances, shops, and transport evolved—slowly shaping what we see today through Taisho era food, coffee, films, and new architecture. Kyoto. With this, history can turn into your next travel plan; let’s start with the Minamiza theater mentioned earlier—I’d photographed it from Shijo Bridge and walked past it countless times, but had never gone inside. It wasn't until I saw the movie.

# 把歷史排進行程：南座與花街表演

"National Treasure" that I suddenly wanted to sit in the theater, so I checked for the next day's show and bought a third-floor seat. I watched a Kamigata comedy that day, not Kabuki, but looking down at the red auditorium and the stage from the third floor, I still felt: "I've finally walked in." The theater building in front of me was largely completed in 1929, featuring a traditional "hafu" gable on the exterior, but the interior? It utilizes modern structural design, lighting, and stage equipment; its 400-year history has seen many building changes, yet it continues to welcome audiences. I later. had the opportunity to enter a Gion Kobu teahouse, watching geiko and maiko performances up close—some dancing, some playing the shamisen—and I finally understood the differences in their hairstyles, flowers, and outfits; the vague impressions from seeing them on the street turned into a concrete appreciation of their professional tradition. Private teahouse banquets require special arrangements, but public performances at Kaburenjo theaters are much easier to fit into a travel itinerary. I also once saw a limited-time performance in Pontocho that combined geiko dance, Japanese. opera, and Gion-matsuri themes; the content changes with each event, so check the schedule beforehand to find a show that interests you. Moving from the theater to daily life, the primary schools mentioned earlier are now accessible to travelers today. For example, the Kyoto International Manga Museum was formerly Tatsuike Primary School. Bookshelves line the old classrooms and hallways, where you can pick up a manga and sit down to read. You might have been stopped by a teacher for reading manga in class before, but now you can buy a ticket to.

# 舊小學校變成漫畫館與旅館

come in and read, while another school has become the Kyoto. Art Center; the corridors still retain a school-like feel, while the classrooms now host exhibitions, creative activities, and cafes. As for the former primary school by the Kamo River, I actually stayed there for a night. The guest rooms are modern hotel facilities. At night, the arches and long windows of the old school building lit up, reminding me of when I came to take photos years ago, back when it was still a closed school. Next to the school gate is a plaque marking the birthplace of Japanese cinema. This land once belonged to the. Kyoto Electric Light Company. In 1897, Seitaro Shibata brought back film projection equipment from France and held trials here. The school moved in later; I originally only meant to stay the night, but ended up encountering the beginnings of Kyoto's film history. If you are looking for a place to have coffee, the Kyoto Prefectural Office Old Main Building is also well worth a visit. Completed in 1904, its facade is symmetrical, with an entrance and grand staircase in the center. Walking inside , you can still see long corridors and exquisite woodwork. Interestingly, although it is called the "Old Main.

# 京都府廳舊本館與老咖啡店

Building," some rooms are still used as office space today. When I went there, aside from seeing the architecture, I also visited the ground-floor cafe, " Salon 1904." The name is taken from the year the building was completed, managed by Maeda Coffee, with white walls, dark wainscoting, and red carpets. There is also furniture that was used in government offices, which now allows guests to sit down and enjoy a coffee. One of the coffees is called "Shigemitsu," named after the building's designer, Matsumuro Shigemitsu. I had originally read his name on an information plaque, and upon. reaching the cafe, I unexpectedly encountered him again on the menu. After finishing a cup, the architect's name was at least much easier to remember. Kyoto's modern life has also left many stories in its old shops, such as Inoda Coffee. In 1940, it originally started as a coffee bean wholesaler, and only opened a cafe after the war in 1947. I once stayed nearby and walked into the main shop for breakfast in the morning. Behind the windowpane were western-style chairs and staff members in white uniforms. The era of war affected. materials and jobs, and also changed many families. Eventually, after the war, some people returned to Kyoto to reopen their shops. One that has a very deep connection with Taiwan is Gion Tsujiri. Walking from Hanamikoji to Shijo-dori, you may have seen their sign or eaten their matcha soft-serve, and the dessert shop upstairs is called Saryo Tsujiri. I originally thought the story of Uji tea should start in Uji, but later realized this shop must also pass through Taipei. The brand originated from a tea merchant in Uji,.

# 祇園辻利與台灣的淵源

Tsujiriemon. Later, Tokusaburo Miyoshi came to Taiwan in 1899 to run the " Tsujiri Tea Shop" in Taipei, where he also researched and promoted Taiwanese tea. He lived in Taiwan for many years, and the next generation of his family grew up there as well. After World War II, the Miyoshi family returned to Japan and reopened the store in Gion, Kyoto, in 1948. The Tokusaburo Miyoshi documents preserved at the Academia Sinica's Institute of Taiwan History also record the relationship between this Taipei tea shop and "Tsujiri." Therefore, behind this familiar Kyoto. brand today lies the journey of a family returning from Taiwan to Japan to rebuild their business. That time, I finally went up to the second floor of the main store and ordered the "Kyoto no Kiwami." The staff first brought cold-brewed tea, then a dessert with matcha ice cream, agar jelly, and shiratama; I just wanted to eat matcha, but ended up reading the history of Taipei from the shop's story. Finally, there is a pair of places that are hundreds of years apart, yet can be understood together. The aforementioned Emperor Go-Mizunoo, many years after his abdication, built the Shugakuin.

# 修學院離宮與京都迎賓館

Imperial Villa in the northeast of Kyoto in his later years. I followed the tour from the Lower Villa, passing through pine trees, paths, and ridges, until reaching the Rinyu-tei, where the Yokuryuchi pond unfolded below. It turns out that a royal villa can incorporate the surrounding rural fields and mountain scenery into the view for visitors. Later, I applied to visit the Kyoto State Guest House within the Kyoto Imperial Palace grounds, and encountered bridges, lacquerware, and plants again. However, this is a national facility that only. opened in 2005 to host foreign heads of state and important guests. Walking through the tour route, you see rooms used for meetings, banquets, and performances in sequence; the woodwork and lacquerware all have different craftsmanship, and I was deeply impressed by the long table in the main dining room. It is a 12-meter table; the black tabletop reflects the window light and looks very formal, but there is space underneath to hang your legs, allowing foreign guests unaccustomed to kneeling to dine more comfortably. I really like this detail, because. entertaining guests ultimately requires considering how they sit and how they will use the space. Four hundred years ago, the receptions held by the Emperor and the Shogun embodied the memories of Kyoto. Today, these crafts continue to be used in different buildings to meet modern needs. If you would like to visit the Kyoto State Guest House in person, you can plan your trip according to the public schedule released by the Cabinet Office. Therefore, much of today’s Kyoto experience for travelers begins in the Edo period. By understanding how it evolved through name changes, one can. better grasp what we see before us now. There are many more stories from this journey, which I have compiled in my newly released book, "Kyoto Times," so please feel free to continue reading if you are interested. Finally, I would like to ask you a few questions: First, have you ever seen a performance in Kyoto? Which one left the deepest impression on you? Second, do you prefer the Kyoto Imperial Palace or the Sento Imperial Palace? Third, which place would you most like to visit on your next trip to Kyoto? Fourth, if you had to pick one scene in Kyoto that seems traditional but actually appeared.

# 結語與留言互動

quite recently, which one would it be? Please leave a comment to let me know and share your thoughts with fellow viewers. Alright, that is all for this episode. Remember to like, subscribe, hit the notification bell, and join the channel membership to stay tuned for more history and travel topics from the "Kyoto Times" perspective. See you next time. Bye.
