https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C7uBvSE3kL8

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入了解坂本龍一被尊稱為「教授」的由來，以及晚年藝術創作轉型的關鍵心路歷程。
  • 全面掌握即將在臺北市立美術館登場的「觀音．聽時」大展核心概念，提前解讀聲音與時間的哲學密碼。
  • 透過資深樂迷工頭堅橫跨台北、東京、大阪的親身追尋視角，感受音樂大師跨越生死藩籬的藝術生命力。

摘要

追尋「教授」坂本龍一的足跡與告別之旅

旅讀總監工頭堅細述了音樂巨擘坂本龍一對其深遠的影響。大師廣為人知的「教授」稱號，源自YMO樂團成員高橋幸宏對當時在東京藝大攻讀碩士的坂本龍一所開的玩笑。工頭堅回顧近年一路追隨大師的足跡：從2019年在台北因電影《你的臉》映後座談得以近距離一睹風采，到大師離世後於2024年配戴MR裝置觀賞虛擬演奏《Kagami》，再到2025年走訪東京現代美術館與大阪美術館參觀展覽。在展場中，作者目睹了重現大師觸鍵力道與呼吸節奏的自動演奏鋼琴與沉浸式光影，這段旅程不僅是回顧，更像是一場漫長而溫柔的告別式。

北美館大展核心：「觀音．聽時」的哲學根源

即將於臺北市立美術館開展的「觀音．聽時」，名稱源自1982年坂本龍一與日本哲學家大森莊藏的六場深度對談。兩人在探討中指出，聲音一旦誕生便注定消亡，而人們所感知的「當下」並非單薄的點，更像是一張略微失焦的照片，同時包容著剛消逝與即將發生的聲響。音樂作為一種「存在於時間中的時間藝術」，這場展覽正是嘗試將抽象的時間與聲音轉化為具象的感知空間，引導觀眾以眼看見聲音、以耳聽見時間的流動。

從旋律到物質：大師晚年藝術觀的深刻轉折

對於創作過《末代皇帝》等經典配樂的大師為何在晚年投身裝置藝術，工頭堅指出其轉折源於兩大關鍵事件：其一是2011年東日本大震災，被海嘯淹沒的鋼琴讓坂本龍一體悟到，人類追求標準音準是傲慢的，而那架走音的鋼琴實為「被自然重新調音」，自此聲音在他眼中化為如同水石般具體的「自然物質」；其二則是對非線性時間的思索，大師逐漸將目光轉向雨滴、海嘯、森林與電波等自然維度。自2017年專輯《async》起，大師正式打破線性時間的束縛，將聲音轉移至實體空間，展開了前衛的跨界藝術實踐。

================================================

# 開場：「教授」的由來

Hello everyone, members and friends, I am your travel director, Kung Tou-chien . Ryuichi Sakamoto’s longtime fans are accustomed to affectionately calling him "Professor." There is an origin to this title; it was given by his YMO bandmate , Yukihiro Takahashi. When they first met, Takahashi learned Sakamoto was still a graduate student at Tokyo University of the Arts and asked, "Are you planning to become a university professor?" He just decided to call him "Professor," and that nickname stuck for. a lifetime. The Professor has been gone for some time now, but I believe we all still miss him dearly. When the Professor passed away three years ago, I made a tribute video for him. It introduced his music and life through different periods, as well as his profound influence on me. Those interested can go back and watch it. Come to think of it, I’ve been chasing the Professor’s work for these past few years. In 2019, I met him in person up close in Taipei. In 2024, I wore a device at the National Theater to watch him perform,. and in 2025, I attended two of his exhibitions in Tokyo and Osaka. The Professor’s largest exhibition, "Seeing with Sound, Hearing with Eyes," will officially open at the Taipei Fine Arts Museum on October 31st, the day after this video goes live. So, I made this special video to give you a comprehensive overview before the exhibition opens. First, I’ll briefly share my years of following the Professor, then focus on the works being shown in Taipei to see what each of them aims to express. This is a sharing of sentiments from one who is also a fan of the Professor. As an aside, many of the Professor’s exhibitions allow photography and filming, which gives more people a chance to get to know these works. However, for the photography rules in Taipei, please follow the official announcements. Also, I’d like to let you know that this video was originally exclusive to members, but this time it will be public for 20 days so more friends can watch it. If you enjoy the way this video is narrated, please be sure to join my channel membership. So, let’s get started. Let’s first rewind to 2018, when the documentary* Ryuichi Sakamoto: Coda*was released in Taiwan, and I went to the theater. The following year, the Professor returned to Taiwan for the first time in 24 years . In early June, he attended a film talk for*Your Face*along with director Tsai Ming-liang. He composed the soundtrack for*Your Face *. That was the only time I saw the Professor up close. Although it was just a fleeting glimpse, I was already very.

# 2018–2019：《終章》與「你的臉＋光」

satisfied. In the spring of 2023, the Professor left us. The following March, the concert film*Ryuichi Sakamoto: Opus *was released in Taiwan. At the same time, the Taiwan International Festival of Arts staged "Kagami" at the National Theater. Wearing a mixed-reality headset , the Professor sits at the center of the stage playing the piano. You can walk right up to him to see his expressions and fingers, as if he were truly performing before your eyes. The experience is incredibly surreal, yet deeply moving. In the spring of 2025, I.

# 2023–2024：《OPUS》與《鏡：KAGAMI》

visited the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo to see "Seeing Sound, Hearing Time ." The line of people waiting to get in stretched all the way outdoors. Rather than just an exhibition, it felt more like attending a very long, drawn-out farewell. Walking in, the first thing that stopped me in my tracks was a glowing object suspended in mid-air. This piece will be shown in Taipei as well; I’ll talk more about it in a moment. There was another room that left a deep impression on me. A massive screen covered the entire wall. Sometimes it showed dark, rolling waves . At other times, beams of horizontal.

# 2025 春：東京都現代美術館

light slowly swept across. The floor reflected the light, appearing as if it were covered in a thin layer of water. Everyone just stood quietly in the dark room watching. I stayed there for quite a while, and as I watched, I felt like shedding a few tears. That autumn, I caught another show at the Osaka Art Museum. It was much smaller, but it took the focus back to when the Professor was 18 . The 1970 Osaka Expo. Back then, the Professor was deeply shaken by a set of metal instruments.

# 2025 秋：大阪

called "sound sculptures." Half a century later, he rediscovered these restored sound sculptures, performed and recorded with them personally, and even used those sounds in his album, "12." Coincidentally, with the 2025 Osaka Expo taking place, it felt like bringing the Professor’s origin back to the same city . In the exhibition, there was also a grand piano that played by itself. No one was sitting in front of it, yet the keys moved one by one. It played everything from "Energy Flow" to the theme from "Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence." It reproduced the Professor’s original touch and intensity from when he was alive, capturing even his breath-like pauses. Standing before the empty piano, I have to say, it felt almost as if he were right there. At the end of that same year, I made a special trip to a theater in Hibiya, Tokyo, to watch "Opus," a documentary centered on the Professor’s journals, chronicling his final three and a half years. Over these past few years, one feeling has remained constant: the Professor is no longer here.

# 2025 年底：《Ryuichi Sakamoto: Diaries》

But his voice and his image still breathe and flow within these exhibition spaces. Beyond the sadness, there is also a sense of healing and peace. Now, let’s move on to the focus of this video: the exhibition in Taipei. First, let’s talk about the exhibition title, " Seeing Sound, Hearing Time." It sounds a bit abstract at first, but the meaning is actually quite beautiful. "Seeing" is to see the sound. "Hearing" is to hear the time. His original Japanese title is " Idiosyncrasy"; the Chinese version.

# 展名「觀音．聽時」的由來

condenses this into four characters. These characters actually have a history , originating from a 1982 collection of dialogues where a 30-year-old Ryuichi Sakamoto sought advice from Japanese philosopher Shozo Omori. It is based on six dialogues between the two regarding sound and time. The Chinese edition of this book was timed to be published alongside the opening of the Taipei exhibition, titled "Observing Sound, Listening to Time." For those who want to delve deeper, I. highly recommend finding a copy to read . You could say that throughout the Professor's life, his work appeared to be music on the surface, but at its core , it was always questioning "what is sound" and "what is time." There is an easy-to-understand example in the book; the Professor said, "Once a sound is born, it is destined to die." Shozo Omori then added that the " present" we perceive is not a point without thickness. It is more like a photograph that is slightly out of focus. It still holds the sound that just. vanished, while also preparing for the next one. The Professor even said that music is a temporal art that exists within time. Alright, let's keep these two keywords in mind: seeing sound and listening to time. Before we look at the seven works in the Taipei exhibition one by one, let me clarify two things. First, where do these explanations come from? Since I am truly a long-time fan of the Professor. Back when he exhibited in Beijing and Chengdu, I already bought the simplified.

# 看作品之前：理解教授晚年的兩把鑰匙

Chinese exhibition catalog online. Later , I went to Tokyo and picked up a thick exhibition handbook with parallel Japanese and English texts. Much of what I will share comes from these catalogs and the curators 'essays , combined with my own insights from his films, digested and retold to you all. For the works I didn't film, I will use publicly available materials from the Taipei Fine Arts Museum. Second, here is a key to understanding these works. Many people might have this question. Why would a maestro who composed the scores. for "The Last Emperor" and "Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence" spend his later years making these installations that seem a bit hard to grasp at first? Even curator Yuko Namba said she was taken aback when she first saw the Professor's installations in 2007. As I delved deeper, I realized the key lies in two events. The first is the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake. After the tsunami, the Professor saw a piano in the disaster zone that had been ruined by seawater. To most people, it was just a piece of junk, but the Professor said it was a piano "retuned by nature." He realized that humans trying so hard to tune a piano to a standard pitch is actually quite arrogant. From then on, sound was, for him, not just melody but also a kind of matter. It is a tangible existence, just like stone or water. This piano later became a work of art. It likely isn't in the Taipei exhibition , but it is the most important starting.

point for understanding the Professor's later years. This process is also presented in the COA documentary. The second point is his obsession with time. We are accustomed to thinking of time as a straight line, moving forward one second at a time. However, could the time of a drop of water, a burst of mist, or a shower actually be fluid and circular? The Professor believed more that time could be many strands, flowing simultaneously , each following its own path. Biologist Shinichi Fukuoka once said that uniform. , forward-moving linear time is actually an invention of the human brain. It is precisely because life resists the decay of all things that we perceive time. Art critic Seiko Shike noted that in his later years, the Professor gradually shifted his creative focus away from people. He went to listen to rain, life , tsunamis, and forests. Even the invisible radio waves within the city. And the 2017 album "async" was a watershed moment. Starting with this album, he moved from exhibiting individual works to curating entire exhibitions, effectively taking music out of the constraints of time. He placed them piece by piece into the space. In fact, as early as a 1982 collection of interviews, the 30-year-old Professor was already talking about music making space visible. These installations 40 years later are the realization of those early ideas: sound is mist, and time flows. Keep these two concepts in mind,.

and you will understand the seven sets of works that follow. Among the seven sets of works in Taipei, three come from the Professor's most important later works. His major collaborator, Shiro Takatani, is a founding member of the Japanese avant-garde art group "Dumb Type," and he created the visuals for the Professor’s opera. In 2022, the Professor officially joined Dumb Type, participating as a member in their constellation at the Japan Pavilion of the Venice Biennale.

# 高谷史郎《LIFE——流動、無形、無聲……》

The first piece is the glowing mist I saw in Tokyo. "Life–Fluid, Invisible, Inaudible." Over a dozen acrylic water tanks create a cloud of mist hanging overhead. Images are projected onto the mist within the tanks; when the mist is dense , the images are clear. When the mist clears, the images pass through. Painting a shimmering pool of light on the floor. These images and sounds are more than 400 fragments from his 1999 opera,. randomly recombined by a computer, so the moment you see it is unique. This opera discusses war and revolution , science and technology, and how humans and nature coexist. It could be called a requiem written for the 20th century. Viewers can stroll beneath it, stand, or even lie down. The second piece is " Water State 1." It is much quieter. In the center of the room is a black pool, its surface like a mirror, surrounded by large stones, with rain.

# 《水的樣態1》

falling from the ceiling into the pool. The rhythm is based on rainfall data from weather satellites. In Tokyo, it uses the exact rainfall of Tokyo for an entire year. The rain transforms into sound, and the lights also change gradually. The ripples on the water sometimes look like the sea viewed from high above. At other times, they look like rain falling into a roadside puddle . I'm curious if it will be changed to Taipei's rain in Taipei. This piece is perfect for finding a corner to sit and watch the water,.

# 《async——沉浸》

immersing yourself in it. It comes from the album*12*, which the Professor completed while battling cancer. In Tokyo, it was displayed on an 18-meter-long massive screen. Accompanied by over a dozen speakers surrounding you. On the screen, the piano, books, and plants in the Professor’s New York studio are woven into images by thin horizontal lines, then slowly disassembled. The visuals and music are not synchronized, each following its own. timeline. This is exactly what "async" means. The curator says this piece provides the closest experience to attending a live performance in the entire exhibition. Next is the work of Japanese new media artist Daito Manabe. Those who like J-Pop have likely already seen his work . Many of the mind-blowing stage visuals at Perfume concerts were created by him and his team, Rhizomatiks.

# 真鍋大度《感測流 2024——不可見、不可聞》

His specialty is turning invisible data into something visible and tangible. His collaboration with the Professor, " sensing streams-invisible, inaudible," first appeared at the 2014 Sapporo International Art Triennale, where the Professor was the guest director. Speaking of that art festival, I actually have a very regretful memory. I had already arrived in Sapporo at the time. The underground malls were filled with art festival posters featuring the Professor's name. But the Professor suddenly couldn't make. it for the performance due to health reasons; it was a real shame to miss it . He was diagnosed with oropharyngeal cancer that year and had to focus on treatment in New York, so the original concert had to be canceled. In Tokyo, this was a 16-meter-long, slim LED screen. Antennas outside the venue capture cell phone, Wi-Fi, and broadcast radio waves in real-time, converting them into images and sound. We are surrounded by these waves every day without feeling them, but this piece turns them into a flowing scene like an. ecosystem. Maybe even the signal from the phone in your pocket gets picked up by it. As a side note, a few days ago, I made a special trip to Taichung to see Daito Manabe's solo exhibition, "Temporal Boundaries." The core of this exhibition is that time is generated by relationships. The entire space is divided into three connected environments. As visitors move through them, they reshape the work's evolution. I've always loved Daito Manabe's work.

# 岔個話：台中「關係時態」

with Perfume; there were few people at the museum that day, making it a unique experience to fully immerse myself. This aligns closely with the professor's idea that time flows, so it’s no wonder they collaborated. The exhibition at the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts runs until early January, and at the Taipei Fine Arts Museum until March, so they can be viewed in succession. The third artist is the German Carsten Nicolai. He works in visual arts while producing electronic music under the name Alva Noto.

# 卡斯滕・尼古拉《光幻視》《內／外》

He has released several albums and toured with the professor, collaborating for over 20 years. These two works are inspired by Jules Verne's "Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea." Nicolai envisioned the novel as a feature film, writing a 24-chapter script. Two chapters are exhibited here, paired with tracks from the professor's final album, "12," each named after the recording date. "Phosphene" refers to the spots of light and afterimages that appear on the inside of the eyelids when you close. your eyes. This corresponds to the chapter where the crew falls into hallucinations due to oxygen deprivation . The professor's synthesizer sounds seem to emerge from deep fog, while the visuals feature vast collections of animal specimens and skeletons from European museums. Set to the professor's slow, melancholic piano, it reflects Captain Nemo’s museum visit before setting sail, quietly questioning the relationship between life, death, and nature. It also reminds us that how museums display items often carries a. gaze inherited from the colonial era. The fourth artist is Thai director Apichatpong Weerasethakul. As a winner of the Cannes Palme d'Or, he held a solo exhibition, "The Serenity of Madness," at the Taipei Fine Arts Museum in 2019, making him an old friend. His collaboration with the professor on " Light" is unique. He gave a "digital toy camera" to friends and family to film freely. The resulting footage shows warm seas and sleeping children and dogs—intimate.

# 阿比查邦《async——初光》《沉睡者》

, daily moments. He selected two tracks and asked the professor to adjust their length to the footage. In the end, set to a poetic play by Arseny Tarkovsky, the people on screen slowly drift off to sleep one by one. Apichatpong describes the professor's music as the first light entering your eyes upon waking at dawn. The other piece, "Sleepers," is Apichatpong's own silent short film, featuring footage that didn't appear in. his film "Memoria." Tilda Swinton’s character slowly falls asleep at the end of her journey. The two are screened together—one beginning with the light of dawn, the other ending with a slumber at the journey's conclusion. The lines between day and night, waking and dreaming, slowly melt together; I highly recommend watching the series in one go. The final async volume collaboration features a member of Ubalan, the professor’s son, directing the concert-setting Opus empty-sound SarNail.

# Zakkubalan《async——容積》

. In the dim room, 24 iPhones and iPads are lined up on the wall like small windows, playing the professor’s creative process. They capture the visuals and sounds of the New York studio living room and garden, intentionally omitting the professor himself, focusing only on the traces and presence he left behind. It is like a portrait of the professor without him actually being in the frame . The windows are small, requiring you to peer into them one by one. When you lean in close to one, the sounds from the others fade away. Everyone hears a different combination, as if secretly peeking into the professor’s inner world; Sora said previous documentaries already captured his daily life. This time, they wanted to recreate what the professor might have seen and heard during his creative process in an intimate, ethereal way; these seven works, plus 1999 opera archives, make up this Taipei exhibition. These documents record how the professor transitioned from the concert stage to. spatial installations; viewing them after the exhibit provides the perfect contrast. I had been looking forward to this since I heard the news and grabbed my tickets early. It is by appointment only; you must select a date and time on OpenTIX. The ticket prices are very generous: 30 for the general public, 15 for students and Taipei residents, and free for those over 65. One account can book up to four tickets for the same slot. There is no time.

# 參觀資訊

limit once you enter, but if you step out, you must rejoin the waiting line to re-enter. So, it is best to use the restroom before going in. Whether you miss the professor or are just curious about how sound can be " seen," I highly recommend visiting in person. This experience of surrendering your entire body to sound cannot be replicated by even the best headphones or high-definition screens. You have to be there to truly understand. A quick reminder: I have presented the currently announced list, but please refer to the. official announcement for the final exhibited works. Walking out of the exhibition, I kept thinking about one thing. We always assume that when someone leaves, they take everything with them. But the professor shows us through these exhibits that as long as these sounds continue to flow and these objects continue to drift, he never really left . I have always remembered one thing the professor said. He said that what truly remains is space , and this space will echo forever; this is how the professor’s final book, "How.

# 結語

Many More Times Will I See the Full Moon ," concludes. He wrote a Latin phrase, "Ars longa, vita brevis," meaning art is eternal, but life is fleeting. I still remember that in 2024, while watching "Mirror" at the National Theater, these very same words were displayed on the grand screen in the lobby. Though he has departed, the works he left behind will remain, echoing on and on. This exhibition, "Sound of Guanyin,. " will be on display in Taipei until March of next year. If you can, I hope you will visit in person to listen to the echoes the professor left in the exhibition hall and find your own emotions and reflections. As a reminder, if you enjoy videos like this, please join as a channel member. I will continue to produce more exclusive member videos in the future. I am Gongtoujian. See you in the next member-exclusive video. Yeah.

item.title: 工頭也答不出來的地方！工友知道嗎？ ft. 蘇巧慧
item.itunes:title: 工頭也答不出來的地方！工友知道嗎？ ft. 蘇巧慧
item.itunes:author: 工頭堅。旅行長
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f6icM4j9qCQ

值得閱讀的理由

  • 結合影視製作經驗與觀光美學，探討如何捕捉具備故事性的單一畫面，打造能深植人心、推動社群傳播的打卡亮點。
  • 借鏡日本東海道宿場演化為東京都會圈的歷史脈絡，對照台灣鐵路開通對新北市29區聚落發展的深遠影響。
  • 從「臥城」與「衛星城市」的刻板印象切入，深入探討新北居民的在地認同，以及各行政區如何邁向自主發光的「恆星」地位。

摘要

影視幕後經驗與視覺打卡美學

作者在節目中邀請立法委員蘇巧慧對談，意外揭開兩人都曾有過影視幕後工作的共同經歷。蘇巧慧在美留學期間曾擔任製片行政統籌，作者則曾從事美術場景設計。蘇巧慧提到，過去的拍片訓練讓她習慣尋找最能傳遞故事的「關鍵畫面」；這項能力也延伸至觀光思維，她認為一個優秀的旅遊景點必須具備能讓人留下深刻記憶的代表性地標與拍照打卡點，才能在社群時代引發共鳴並吸引旅人重複造訪。

從東海道宿場看新北衛城的歷史脈絡

作者分享自己走訪日本東海道的經驗，提及連結京都與江戶的古代宿場，隨著鐵路通車逐漸演變成環繞東京的衛星城市（臥城），這與新北市的發展軌跡極為相似。新北市擁有29個行政區，包含作者在內的許多居民都是從外地移居至此並落地生根。如同日本各宿場因鐵路開通與否而走向不同命運，新北各區的繁榮也深深受到交通動線與歷史演進的影響。

打破附庸定位：從衛星蛻變為獨立恆星

針對新北市常被視為台北市附庸的現象，兩人深入討論了「衛星變恆星」的概念。蘇巧慧強調，沒有地方願意永遠只做圍繞他人旋轉的衛星，每個市鎮都期盼能成為主宰自身發展的主體。她指出台灣早期歷史便有「一府、二鹿、三新莊」的說法，證明新北地區早具備深厚的歷史地位與主體性，未來更應善用自身特色，發展成自主發光的燦爛恆星。

Yes, so I think our diversity is our unique feature, and we must use our unique features to win everyone’s recognition. This is my vision and expectation for New Taipei City, and it is also the goal I am working towards. So, in this process, regarding the connections with foreign cities you just mentioned—whether through mutual cooperation, creating new things to be. seen, or using others as a reference to help us become......objects of interest , I think this is also a method. It's all about the approach. So, since you’re a Japan expert who wants to re-examine New Taipei from a Japanese perspective today, I really look forward to the opportunity on this show to share with all my friends who love visiting Japan that New Taipei actually has many wonderful attractions. Of course, I know that New Taipei’s. attractions still need a bit more effort, for instance, transportation to these spots. >> It needs to be more comfortable. Take the hiking trails we just mentioned; I feel that the transport links to get to those trails are not very convenient in New Taipei right now. After taking the MRT, you still need to transfer to a bus to reach the trailhead. After finishing a hike, going from point A to point B sometimes doesn't get you home smoothly. Just thinking, "I finally. finished the hike, do I really have to hike all the way back?" You just decide , forget it, I won't go. >> And it's not suitable to drive, because your car is parked at one point, and... right. Exactly. So these are all issues that we, as a government...... >> agency, should be able to improve, and only then can these attractions be more liked and accepted by everyone. Like the bike paths we mentioned earlier, the nodes along the way should be well-designed. And of course, this includes the city itself, which has too. many historical stories—how do we dig them up to make them interesting? For example, I should find experts like you , or even collaborate with the film and television industry; do you know how many there are? >> That’s what I wanted to say. It doesn't have to be just me. Yes, a lot of our yearning for or understanding of Japanese attractions comes from anime and movies. Exactly. >> I think more movies should be filmed in New Taipei. New Taipei has so many stories and settings, which also fits. what you said about needing to be " Instagrammable." >> For instance, even advertisements could work; it doesn't have to be limited to film and TV works. Variety shows could also work, right? You can do anything here; for instance, our coast with its three layers of sea could host the best challenge-based or stamina-testing programs, right? Sports competitions should definitely come here, like the Gongliao Triathlon or the North Coast Triathlon—they are amazing, aren't they? And take, for example, how everyone currently only thinks of Jiufen for filming "Dust in the Wind," >> or "A City of Sadness." >> And, even though Hayao Miyazaki himself denied it, everyone still thinks those are the scenes from "Spirited Away." >> You didn't know the street scenes in " Wave Makers" were filmed in Sanchong? I did. >> So, there are actually many more scenes filmed in New Taipei City, and it can be presented in diverse ways, but I hope it serves as more than just a filming location. >> I hope it can actually become the birthplace of stories. >> Mm. >> I think that would be even better; for example, our Jide Temple in Xizhi is. where "The Teenage Psychic" originated. >> Oh, really? Yes, yes, Liu Bo-jun— that’s the place where that story originated. So for us, Jide Temple eventually gained some visibility. People will come here out of curiosity and interest, and once they visit, they’ll end up loving it. The public sector can help these stories be seen; for example, I want to make New Taipei City the most film-friendly city. >> By being the friendliest place to film and encouraging everyone to come, more works will naturally be born from this city of New Taipei. That is my approach , and including what we just discussed, my ultimate dream is to let the unique characteristics of every district be seen, to have everyone appreciate the strengths of each district, and for people in every district to take pride in where they come from. "I am a Gongliao local, I am a Pingxi local, I. am a Zhonghe local, I am a Yingge local "—I want every child in every district to feel, "Yes, that’s right, I’m from Wulai." That feeling is exactly what I want, but when these 29 districts come together, >> Mm. >> I am a New Taipei citizen. >> Right. >> I am from Greater New Taipei. >> If you go to Japan in the future and tell people you are from New Taipei, they won't be surprised; they are very clear about this. >> I am from, well, bigger than Taipei, the "New" Taipei. >> A place that is bigger and more diversely developed than Taipei. >> Yes, yes, yes. Well, I feel that after our conversation today, I’m immediately inspired to make another video. Because we talked about a lot, whether it’s the unique features of each district or the comparison between New Taipei and Japan's tertiary cities, I don't think we can finish today, as I know the committee member has a busy schedule. But I promise everyone that I will turn this topic into another video.

# 結語與「新北照片」募集

to bring the vision in my head to life for everyone to see. I really feel that many things can be turned into better travel experiences, or even using tourism to get to know this city; that’s actually one of our goals and methods. Hearing this from you, I am very gratified. Why? Because I know that if one is truly serving as a leader, just dealing with civil administration issues is already. extremely busy, and then being expected to take care of tourism and city diplomacy. I almost feel bad for them. No, no, not at all. I actually think that things like travel and tourism are the best areas of expertise for this era. I’ll say it again, my goal is to achieve balanced identity for all 29 districts of New Taipei City, so in some places we rely on developing manufacturing to help them thrive and. grow better. >> But in other places we rely on tourism, and actually, for any place, I think it’s worth using tourism as a way to introduce ourselves to others, to let more people know us—is there any better way than this? So, tourism experts are the important consultants and key figures I really hope to bring together in the future. >> Sounds like we’ll have plenty of opportunities to meet in the future. That’s right, that was the plan all. along. I’m running in this election for this goal, not just to win the campaign. I hope this era allows the allocation of public resources to move in line with the pulse of the new era that I feel. I came with this hope, and I hope to call upon more people to join us. As for me, I just want to have a sense of pride and identity as a citizen, and I can use my expertise to contribute some things for it. >> Yes, and you can contribute your part, you can start by introducing Yonghe, that’s right. >> You can start by introducing Yonghe. >> Very fitting, very fitting. Wow, we actually prepared so much, and we could go on forever because, honestly, there are just so many places in New Taipei City that mirror these Japanese local lines. We are very happy to have invited Legislator Chiao, who is also a candidate for Mayor of New Taipei City, to our show today. I hope that shortly after this episode airs, everything we've talked about can come true. Thank. you everyone. I’m also very glad to have this opportunity today. I actually thought about asking your audience to collect photos of places that look like they’re somewhere else, but are actually in New Taipei, >> We can collect them, absolutely. Really ? Yes! So, I want to say this to the camera: to all our listeners and viewers, I’m really looking forward to it. If you know of more great places in New Taipei, could you share them with me? Even those spots where you thought, "I thought this was somewhere in Japan," or "I thought this was somewhere else," but it’s actually in New Taipei, could you share those? I. really want to know, and in the future, I will definitely make sure more people get to see these places. We can turn this into a hashtag, whether on IG or YT, that works too. Alright, thank you all for watching today. I'm Gong Tou-jian, and we'll see you next time on our podcast. >> See you next time! I hope I can come back often to share more about New Taipei with everyone.

item.description:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f6icM4j9qCQ

值得閱讀的理由

  • 結合影視製作經驗與觀光美學，探討如何捕捉具備故事性的單一畫面，打造能深植人心、推動社群傳播的打卡亮點。
  • 借鏡日本東海道宿場演化為東京都會圈的歷史脈絡，對照台灣鐵路開通對新北市29區聚落發展的深遠影響。
  • 從「臥城」與「衛星城市」的刻板印象切入，深入探討新北居民的在地認同，以及各行政區如何邁向自主發光的「恆星」地位。

摘要

影視幕後經驗與視覺打卡美學

作者在節目中邀請立法委員蘇巧慧對談，意外揭開兩人都曾有過影視幕後工作的共同經歷。蘇巧慧在美留學期間曾擔任製片行政統籌，作者則曾從事美術場景設計。蘇巧慧提到，過去的拍片訓練讓她習慣尋找最能傳遞故事的「關鍵畫面」；這項能力也延伸至觀光思維，她認為一個優秀的旅遊景點必須具備能讓人留下深刻記憶的代表性地標與拍照打卡點，才能在社群時代引發共鳴並吸引旅人重複造訪。

從東海道宿場看新北衛城的歷史脈絡

作者分享自己走訪日本東海道的經驗，提及連結京都與江戶的古代宿場，隨著鐵路通車逐漸演變成環繞東京的衛星城市（臥城），這與新北市的發展軌跡極為相似。新北市擁有29個行政區，包含作者在內的許多居民都是從外地移居至此並落地生根。如同日本各宿場因鐵路開通與否而走向不同命運，新北各區的繁榮也深深受到交通動線與歷史演進的影響。

打破附庸定位：從衛星蛻變為獨立恆星

針對新北市常被視為台北市附庸的現象，兩人深入討論了「衛星變恆星」的概念。蘇巧慧強調，沒有地方願意永遠只做圍繞他人旋轉的衛星，每個市鎮都期盼能成為主宰自身發展的主體。她指出台灣早期歷史便有「一府、二鹿、三新莊」的說法，證明新北地區早具備深厚的歷史地位與主體性，未來更應善用自身特色，發展成自主發光的燦爛恆星。

================================================

# 精華：你以為在日本，其實在新北

If we talk about New Taipei City, it's like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. That's one way to put it, it's a bit of a metaphor, yes, exactly. If you know of any other great spots in New Taipei City, could you share them with me? Even places that look like they're in Japan but are actually right here in New Taipei, could you share those too? I really want to know. Everyone wants to share the scenes they experience there with others, so being able to photograph these spots is really. important, I think. >> As I just mentioned, that's an abstract ideal, a wish of mine. But in plain terms, it just means you should be able to find what you want anywhere. Hello everyone, I’m your Chief Traveler, Kung Tung-chien. I mentioned last time that our channel would start hosting podcast-style conversations again, since we’ve done them before and are now bringing them back. We already had one guest for a conversation, and I believe many of you have already seen that video. Today, wow, I’m quite happy to discuss this topic because.

# 開場：新北是台北的 Bed Town？

last time, our conversation ended up revolving around the loneliness of modern people. >> Especially the loneliness of people in my generation—it got a bit sentimental toward the end. But today, I feel much happier because many of our viewers love traveling to Japan. That’s right, we’re going to talk about a topic related to traveling in Japan today. As you all know, over the last year or two—or rather, since the beginning of this year—I’ve been traveling the Tokaido in Japan. The Tokaido is the old road that ran from. Kyoto to Edo, and many people used this ancient route to reach Edo, which is today's Tokyo. But you’ll notice that not everyone lives in the heart of Tokyo; many people actually live in the surrounding prefectures. These are the so-called "bedroom towns" where people commute in the morning and return to sleep at night. As a resident of New Taipei City, I realized that where I live is a bit like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. This is our topic for today, and who better to. discuss it with than our guest? We’ve invited Legislative Yuan member Su Chiao-hui to join us today. Thank you, Kung Tung-chien. Hello to all the viewers, I am Otter Mom. >> When Otter Mom tells stories to children, she's "Otter Mom." >> Otter Mom is very well-known. >> Yes, yes, thank you everyone. >> So, Otter Mom also often takes everyone out on trips! >> Alright, as I mentioned earlier, while today's topic is travel-related, seeing you today made me think of something.

# 來賓登場與兩人的片場往事

that probably 99%of our audience doesn't know. We're usually so transparent, is there really something people don't know? >> We share a common experience. I heard that during the years you were studying law in the US, you worked part-time on film sets—first helping your husband with student productions in Texas—and you've even said that you were the best free labor back then. >> Oh, if you want to talk about that, are you asking if I worked as a production assistant? >> We started filming back in college, yeah, we've been filming since our. college days. Basically, it started with him as a student director and me behind the lens—wait, he was behind the lens, and I did everything else besides that, all the administrative work. So you could call me the co-producer. >> That's the truth. >> Right, you could call me an admin assistant, or a producer, anything really; it was just a two-person team, after all. OK, the reason I ask is because many people only know Janet from her days as a "travel expert," but folks, Janet was also in the film industry when she was younger. >> Really? Yes. >> I was doing production design back then , so that included building sets and everything. >> I think production design is just amazing. >> It's so exhausting. >> Production design is truly incredible. You see, they can create that entire scene from scratch. We had a famous saying back then: everything outside the camera frame is fake. Exactly, and later on, I saw how AI is so advanced now, right? A lot of things are done with green screens and computer-generated animation. >> Oh, but it's not the same. I felt that back then, production design could manage everything inside the frame,. from the color coordination to—and I'm very impressed by this—everything from the curtains and dining tables to the table runners. Even the creases in the table runners. Yes. >> Everything had to be perfectly aligned with the director's vision before the actors stepped in and we called "camera ." So, since you're so particular about the visuals, I have a sudden question: when you go to a place now, is your first thought whether it's a good spot to film? Yes.

# 用拍片的眼光看景點：一定要有打卡點

>> Honestly, yes. I truly believe that where we've been leaves a mark, and no experience is ever wasted. I really enjoy having studied law; I feel that my ability to analyze, break down, and synthesize logic and situations has been incredibly helpful, making me much more efficient at handling things now and easier to grasp the crux of an issue. And I feel that in this realm of filming and producing movies, I've also learned a great deal from every single role in the process, since making a. movie is a collaborative effort. For instance, whenever I see a scene now, I find myself thinking about which spot or which angle is the one I want most —if I could only take one photo. >> What is the specific shot that could capture the scene before me and turn it into a story to tell others? >> Or, what is the final image I want to leave behind from this press conference ? >> This idea of deciding what final image I want to capture in a place has almost. become a standard procedure for me, or perhaps, is it >> a kind of pursuit? >> Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. So, I feel that when I look at a scenic spot now, if I ever have the chance to, say, develop a tourism industry, I would really want to create that one specific image that stays in people's hearts. I believe that when there's an image that sticks with visitors, they'll come back a second, third, or fourth time, and bring even more people with them. >> Absolutely, and I have to add one more. point. Because nowadays, everyone has social media—whether it's Instagram, or like me, doing YouTube—everyone wants to share the image of where they are with others, so being able to photograph a spot is really important. >> What I said earlier was an abstract ideal, my wish, but in plain terms, it just means that every place needs a landmark photo spot that makes people want to come back. >> Whether it's natural or man-made, nowadays, it's all about that photo op. It's a must! Which leads us to our topic today: it's essentially a conversation between two New Taipei City residents. >> But in fact, many New Taipei residents are likely just like us; I was born in Yilan, moved to Taipei with my grandfather, and then my father moved us to New Taipei. Many New Taipei residents weren't necessarily born here , but it's precisely because of this that people from all different counties.

# 從東海道宿場談到「衛星變繁星」

and cities live here. >> Exactly. >> We finally, or I should say, we eventually came to treat this place as a—that’s wonderful. Hearing you say that makes us very happy. Yes. >> Really, really, really. Maybe people moved here at first because the housing prices over there were too high to afford, but after moving, they really started to treat this place as their home. Returning to what I mentioned earlier, I’m currently walking the Tokaido. People might still have the impression of the Tokaido as a place in period dramas where feudal lords are. carried in palanquins, but having reached the final stretch, I’ve found that what I’ve seen the most along the way are post stations. These so-called post stations were where people used to stay; after walking for a stretch, they needed a place to stop for the night, so these stations naturally formed settlements. >> Those post stations have now become satellite cities around Tokyo, gradually developing from those original settlements. When Japan began building its railways, the first line. ran from Shimbashi to Yokohama, and then it extended along what is known as the Tokaido, connecting all these post stations. If you look at this narrative , it’s actually exactly the same in Taiwan. >> Exactly the same. >> Exactly the same; our historical development is almost identical. >> Yes, and the railway line, what used to be the main thoroughfare, is now the railway line, and many people from the south traveled up along it. Now, what I want to say is... >> Around us now, it has actually developed around Taipei into... >> How many districts are there in total? 29 districts. In New Taipei City? 29 districts, yes. >> New Taipei City now has 29 districts. Some districts flourished because the railway passed through them. >> But there are also some districts that, like in Japan or in the central region, refused to let the railway pass through back then. After refusing the railway, their prosperity is quite different today. Why I specifically noticed this is because I found that you once talked about a topic called "Satellites. becoming Fixed Stars." >> We mentioned earlier that these surrounding cities seem to just be satellite cities, but as citizens, we naturally hope they aren't*just* satellites. Of course. Everyone wants to be the bright star themselves, to be the main body, not the one revolving around others. I think this is the desire that everyone has—to have the opportunity to be in charge, to be their own master. So when people talk about satellites, it's like revolving. around another star, right? Your speed and your state are likely more constrained by others. I think it's like this: if you look at our New Taipei, the administrative districts weren't drawn like this in the past, so we used to say "one Fu, two Lu, three Zhuang"—and Zhuang refers to Xinzhuang. >> That's the first time I've heard "three ". People nowadays might prefer hearing "three Jia", but it's actually " Xinzhuang" first. It was only after the river channel in Xinzhuang silted up. that things shifted to the deeper Mengjia area. So Xinzhuang is really the place where our ancestors first landed and pioneered, hence the name Xinzhuang. >> Right, actually the names Xinzhuang and Shinjuku are somewhat similar. Somewhat similar, yes. It started along the river, and gradually, as we settled in flatter areas, formed communities, and began farming, our clans and tribes slowly evolved. >> Take Shulin as an example, actually... >> The place where I serve, Shulin—if you just look at its place names, it’s actually very interesting. >> Really? >> Yes, but Shulin is further divided into what are now neighborhood names. >> Because of its ancient place names; I'll start by introducing a central point called Tandi. >> Right, right, so there must have been a pond there. OK, OK. >> That's where people with the surname.

# 樹林古地名與鐵道的由來

Peng started living, they lived there. >> Right. >> Raising ducks. >> And then, gradually, it reached Shanjia . " >> Under the mountain," because as we moved out of the pond area, houses started appearing at the foot of the mountain, hence Shanjia, which is around the current Shanjia Station. >> Right. >> I love hearing this. Yes, and then after you pass that and cross the mountain, it becomes a vast flat area; because they grew oranges there, it's called... >> Oh. >> So that's where it comes from. >> Because I'm really not familiar with the Shulin area. For me, I'm sharing this by using the place where I've served for ten years to show that our ancient place names really reflect the footprints left by our ancestors when they first arrived to conduct various commercial or reclamation activities, and they named them accordingly. That's how we got the current administrative districts, but these districts still. have to evolve along with our development. Ah, so when you said some people accepted the railway while others didn't, it’s not quite like that. The railways back then were built for specific purposes. In my area, Shulin, my neighborhood of Sanjia was actually a coal mining hub at the time. >> Oh, so that’s why it had a station. Exactly. They built the railway to transport coal out from the mines. It ran from Sanjia Station all the way to Shulin Station. Since our area in Ganyuan has vast flatlands that produced the best rice, it was even. classified as a special agricultural zone. Because the quality was so high, the rice had to be shipped out, which is why we have Shulin Station. That’s our origin story. The railway had to be built here because of the produce. Because the goods were here, the railway followed, which is why we developed so early on. But of course, because times have changed, these products are no longer the most essential goods today. Naturally, just. like places like Jiufen or Jinguashi, they’ve faded a bit because there are different business models now. So, how do we create new opportunities for these places so they can find their place again? Since they already have the railway infrastructure, figuring out how to work with their current conditions is the challenge for us today. >> OK, I was listening so intently just now, because I really love hearing stories like this. As you all know, I’ve been doing these historical. walking tours, mainly focused on Japan. This brings me to something I’ve been thinking about a lot these past few years. I’m a resident of New Taipei City, though most of my work is based in Taipei. Mm. >> But the thing is, when we go to Tokyo, you’ll notice that the stations surrounding Tokyo have massive passenger traffic every morning and evening. Why? Because people live right next to them. >> We do too, which is why I even built a station called Pengming Station.

# 新北一市，對應東京周邊三縣

>> That’s right, exactly. >> Beyond the daily commute, these surrounding areas are also where Tokyo residents go for tourism and relaxation . >> So I’ve been imagining—since I used to like comparing Japan to Taiwan in my videos, like how I once compared Kyushu to Taiwan—if we look at New Taipei City, it’s like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. New Taipei is, well, it's like three counties combined,. because New Taipei surrounds Taipei. >> It has both mountains and the sea, and I don't know if you've thought about this, if you often travel to Japan, >> Look, I always keep mine covered. It’s no wonder, your mobile phone wallpaper is a map of New Taipei City. >> Let me tell you a secret, I also used a New Taipei City map as my computer desktop background before. >> Exactly, exactly. No, I think, I think it’s about finding that sense of belonging, which is why we talked about treating this place as home earlier. Right, back to what I was saying, I’ve been making comparisons, so has. everyone noticed that around Tokyo, there’s Chiba Prefecture, Saitama Prefecture, and Kanagawa Prefecture? These are all places that many Taiwanese people love to visit. >> That's right. Take Kanagawa Prefecture for example, since it’s closer to the sea, so simply put, if there’s a comparison to be made, Tamsui could correspond to Yokohama. Some might think, shouldn’t Yokohama correspond to Keelung? No, no, no. Actually, if you look at the earliest ports of the capital, Tamsui should correspond to. Yokohama. >> And then, they have an ancient city called Kamakura, plus another train line that everyone loves to ride and take photos of—the Enoden line. What I want to discuss with you is, how should New Taipei City correspond to these Japanese prefectures and cities in the future? For instance, during your interpellation, you mentioned that the Jiufen-Jinguashi bus route has 5.92 million passengers a year, while I’ve participated in the Crown North Coast route, which only has 38,000. item.content:encoded:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f6icM4j9qCQ

值得閱讀的理由

  • 結合影視製作經驗與觀光美學，探討如何捕捉具備故事性的單一畫面，打造能深植人心、推動社群傳播的打卡亮點。
  • 借鏡日本東海道宿場演化為東京都會圈的歷史脈絡，對照台灣鐵路開通對新北市29區聚落發展的深遠影響。
  • 從「臥城」與「衛星城市」的刻板印象切入，深入探討新北居民的在地認同，以及各行政區如何邁向自主發光的「恆星」地位。

摘要

影視幕後經驗與視覺打卡美學

作者在節目中邀請立法委員蘇巧慧對談，意外揭開兩人都曾有過影視幕後工作的共同經歷。蘇巧慧在美留學期間曾擔任製片行政統籌，作者則曾從事美術場景設計。蘇巧慧提到，過去的拍片訓練讓她習慣尋找最能傳遞故事的「關鍵畫面」；這項能力也延伸至觀光思維，她認為一個優秀的旅遊景點必須具備能讓人留下深刻記憶的代表性地標與拍照打卡點，才能在社群時代引發共鳴並吸引旅人重複造訪。

從東海道宿場看新北衛城的歷史脈絡

作者分享自己走訪日本東海道的經驗，提及連結京都與江戶的古代宿場，隨著鐵路通車逐漸演變成環繞東京的衛星城市（臥城），這與新北市的發展軌跡極為相似。新北市擁有29個行政區，包含作者在內的許多居民都是從外地移居至此並落地生根。如同日本各宿場因鐵路開通與否而走向不同命運，新北各區的繁榮也深深受到交通動線與歷史演進的影響。

打破附庸定位：從衛星蛻變為獨立恆星

針對新北市常被視為台北市附庸的現象，兩人深入討論了「衛星變恆星」的概念。蘇巧慧強調，沒有地方願意永遠只做圍繞他人旋轉的衛星，每個市鎮都期盼能成為主宰自身發展的主體。她指出台灣早期歷史便有「一府、二鹿、三新莊」的說法，證明新北地區早具備深厚的歷史地位與主體性，未來更應善用自身特色，發展成自主發光的燦爛恆星。

================================================

# 精華：你以為在日本，其實在新北

If we talk about New Taipei City, it's like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. That's one way to put it, it's a bit of a metaphor, yes, exactly. If you know of any other great spots in New Taipei City, could you share them with me? Even places that look like they're in Japan but are actually right here in New Taipei, could you share those too? I really want to know. Everyone wants to share the scenes they experience there with others, so being able to photograph these spots is really. important, I think. >> As I just mentioned, that's an abstract ideal, a wish of mine. But in plain terms, it just means you should be able to find what you want anywhere. Hello everyone, I’m your Chief Traveler, Kung Tung-chien. I mentioned last time that our channel would start hosting podcast-style conversations again, since we’ve done them before and are now bringing them back. We already had one guest for a conversation, and I believe many of you have already seen that video. Today, wow, I’m quite happy to discuss this topic because.

# 開場：新北是台北的 Bed Town？

last time, our conversation ended up revolving around the loneliness of modern people. >> Especially the loneliness of people in my generation—it got a bit sentimental toward the end. But today, I feel much happier because many of our viewers love traveling to Japan. That’s right, we’re going to talk about a topic related to traveling in Japan today. As you all know, over the last year or two—or rather, since the beginning of this year—I’ve been traveling the Tokaido in Japan. The Tokaido is the old road that ran from. Kyoto to Edo, and many people used this ancient route to reach Edo, which is today's Tokyo. But you’ll notice that not everyone lives in the heart of Tokyo; many people actually live in the surrounding prefectures. These are the so-called "bedroom towns" where people commute in the morning and return to sleep at night. As a resident of New Taipei City, I realized that where I live is a bit like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. This is our topic for today, and who better to. discuss it with than our guest? We’ve invited Legislative Yuan member Su Chiao-hui to join us today. Thank you, Kung Tung-chien. Hello to all the viewers, I am Otter Mom. >> When Otter Mom tells stories to children, she's "Otter Mom." >> Otter Mom is very well-known. >> Yes, yes, thank you everyone. >> So, Otter Mom also often takes everyone out on trips! >> Alright, as I mentioned earlier, while today's topic is travel-related, seeing you today made me think of something.

# 來賓登場與兩人的片場往事

that probably 99%of our audience doesn't know. We're usually so transparent, is there really something people don't know? >> We share a common experience. I heard that during the years you were studying law in the US, you worked part-time on film sets—first helping your husband with student productions in Texas—and you've even said that you were the best free labor back then. >> Oh, if you want to talk about that, are you asking if I worked as a production assistant? >> We started filming back in college, yeah, we've been filming since our. college days. Basically, it started with him as a student director and me behind the lens—wait, he was behind the lens, and I did everything else besides that, all the administrative work. So you could call me the co-producer. >> That's the truth. >> Right, you could call me an admin assistant, or a producer, anything really; it was just a two-person team, after all. OK, the reason I ask is because many people only know Janet from her days as a "travel expert," but folks, Janet was also in the film industry when she was younger. >> Really? Yes. >> I was doing production design back then , so that included building sets and everything. >> I think production design is just amazing. >> It's so exhausting. >> Production design is truly incredible. You see, they can create that entire scene from scratch. We had a famous saying back then: everything outside the camera frame is fake. Exactly, and later on, I saw how AI is so advanced now, right? A lot of things are done with green screens and computer-generated animation. >> Oh, but it's not the same. I felt that back then, production design could manage everything inside the frame,. from the color coordination to—and I'm very impressed by this—everything from the curtains and dining tables to the table runners. Even the creases in the table runners. Yes. >> Everything had to be perfectly aligned with the director's vision before the actors stepped in and we called "camera ." So, since you're so particular about the visuals, I have a sudden question: when you go to a place now, is your first thought whether it's a good spot to film? Yes.

# 用拍片的眼光看景點：一定要有打卡點

>> Honestly, yes. I truly believe that where we've been leaves a mark, and no experience is ever wasted. I really enjoy having studied law; I feel that my ability to analyze, break down, and synthesize logic and situations has been incredibly helpful, making me much more efficient at handling things now and easier to grasp the crux of an issue. And I feel that in this realm of filming and producing movies, I've also learned a great deal from every single role in the process, since making a. movie is a collaborative effort. For instance, whenever I see a scene now, I find myself thinking about which spot or which angle is the one I want most —if I could only take one photo. >> What is the specific shot that could capture the scene before me and turn it into a story to tell others? >> Or, what is the final image I want to leave behind from this press conference ? >> This idea of deciding what final image I want to capture in a place has almost. become a standard procedure for me, or perhaps, is it >> a kind of pursuit? >> Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. So, I feel that when I look at a scenic spot now, if I ever have the chance to, say, develop a tourism industry, I would really want to create that one specific image that stays in people's hearts. I believe that when there's an image that sticks with visitors, they'll come back a second, third, or fourth time, and bring even more people with them. >> Absolutely, and I have to add one more. point. Because nowadays, everyone has social media—whether it's Instagram, or like me, doing YouTube—everyone wants to share the image of where they are with others, so being able to photograph a spot is really important. >> What I said earlier was an abstract ideal, my wish, but in plain terms, it just means that every place needs a landmark photo spot that makes people want to come back. >> Whether it's natural or man-made, nowadays, it's all about that photo op. It's a must! Which leads us to our topic today: it's essentially a conversation between two New Taipei City residents. >> But in fact, many New Taipei residents are likely just like us; I was born in Yilan, moved to Taipei with my grandfather, and then my father moved us to New Taipei. Many New Taipei residents weren't necessarily born here , but it's precisely because of this that people from all different counties.

# 從東海道宿場談到「衛星變繁星」

and cities live here. >> Exactly. >> We finally, or I should say, we eventually came to treat this place as a—that’s wonderful. Hearing you say that makes us very happy. Yes. >> Really, really, really. Maybe people moved here at first because the housing prices over there were too high to afford, but after moving, they really started to treat this place as their home. Returning to what I mentioned earlier, I’m currently walking the Tokaido. People might still have the impression of the Tokaido as a place in period dramas where feudal lords are. carried in palanquins, but having reached the final stretch, I’ve found that what I’ve seen the most along the way are post stations. These so-called post stations were where people used to stay; after walking for a stretch, they needed a place to stop for the night, so these stations naturally formed settlements. >> Those post stations have now become satellite cities around Tokyo, gradually developing from those original settlements. When Japan began building its railways, the first line. ran from Shimbashi to Yokohama, and then it extended along what is known as the Tokaido, connecting all these post stations. If you look at this narrative , it’s actually exactly the same in Taiwan. >> Exactly the same. >> Exactly the same; our historical development is almost identical. >> Yes, and the railway line, what used to be the main thoroughfare, is now the railway line, and many people from the south traveled up along it. Now, what I want to say is... >> Around us now, it has actually developed around Taipei into... >> How many districts are there in total? 29 districts. In New Taipei City? 29 districts, yes. >> New Taipei City now has 29 districts. Some districts flourished because the railway passed through them. >> But there are also some districts that, like in Japan or in the central region, refused to let the railway pass through back then. After refusing the railway, their prosperity is quite different today. Why I specifically noticed this is because I found that you once talked about a topic called "Satellites. becoming Fixed Stars." >> We mentioned earlier that these surrounding cities seem to just be satellite cities, but as citizens, we naturally hope they aren't*just* satellites. Of course. Everyone wants to be the bright star themselves, to be the main body, not the one revolving around others. I think this is the desire that everyone has—to have the opportunity to be in charge, to be their own master. So when people talk about satellites, it's like revolving. around another star, right? Your speed and your state are likely more constrained by others. I think it's like this: if you look at our New Taipei, the administrative districts weren't drawn like this in the past, so we used to say "one Fu, two Lu, three Zhuang"—and Zhuang refers to Xinzhuang. >> That's the first time I've heard "three ". People nowadays might prefer hearing "three Jia", but it's actually " Xinzhuang" first. It was only after the river channel in Xinzhuang silted up. that things shifted to the deeper Mengjia area. So Xinzhuang is really the place where our ancestors first landed and pioneered, hence the name Xinzhuang. >> Right, actually the names Xinzhuang and Shinjuku are somewhat similar. Somewhat similar, yes. It started along the river, and gradually, as we settled in flatter areas, formed communities, and began farming, our clans and tribes slowly evolved. >> Take Shulin as an example, actually... >> The place where I serve, Shulin—if you just look at its place names, it’s actually very interesting. >> Really? >> Yes, but Shulin is further divided into what are now neighborhood names. >> Because of its ancient place names; I'll start by introducing a central point called Tandi. >> Right, right, so there must have been a pond there. OK, OK. >> That's where people with the surname.

# 樹林古地名與鐵道的由來

Peng started living, they lived there. >> Right. >> Raising ducks. >> And then, gradually, it reached Shanjia . " >> Under the mountain," because as we moved out of the pond area, houses started appearing at the foot of the mountain, hence Shanjia, which is around the current Shanjia Station. >> Right. >> I love hearing this. Yes, and then after you pass that and cross the mountain, it becomes a vast flat area; because they grew oranges there, it's called... >> Oh. >> So that's where it comes from. >> Because I'm really not familiar with the Shulin area. For me, I'm sharing this by using the place where I've served for ten years to show that our ancient place names really reflect the footprints left by our ancestors when they first arrived to conduct various commercial or reclamation activities, and they named them accordingly. That's how we got the current administrative districts, but these districts still. have to evolve along with our development. Ah, so when you said some people accepted the railway while others didn't, it’s not quite like that. The railways back then were built for specific purposes. In my area, Shulin, my neighborhood of Sanjia was actually a coal mining hub at the time. >> Oh, so that’s why it had a station. Exactly. They built the railway to transport coal out from the mines. It ran from Sanjia Station all the way to Shulin Station. Since our area in Ganyuan has vast flatlands that produced the best rice, it was even. classified as a special agricultural zone. Because the quality was so high, the rice had to be shipped out, which is why we have Shulin Station. That’s our origin story. The railway had to be built here because of the produce. Because the goods were here, the railway followed, which is why we developed so early on. But of course, because times have changed, these products are no longer the most essential goods today. Naturally, just. like places like Jiufen or Jinguashi, they’ve faded a bit because there are different business models now. So, how do we create new opportunities for these places so they can find their place again? Since they already have the railway infrastructure, figuring out how to work with their current conditions is the challenge for us today. >> OK, I was listening so intently just now, because I really love hearing stories like this. As you all know, I’ve been doing these historical. walking tours, mainly focused on Japan. This brings me to something I’ve been thinking about a lot these past few years. I’m a resident of New Taipei City, though most of my work is based in Taipei. Mm. >> But the thing is, when we go to Tokyo, you’ll notice that the stations surrounding Tokyo have massive passenger traffic every morning and evening. Why? Because people live right next to them. >> We do too, which is why I even built a station called Pengming Station.

# 新北一市，對應東京周邊三縣

>> That’s right, exactly. >> Beyond the daily commute, these surrounding areas are also where Tokyo residents go for tourism and relaxation . >> So I’ve been imagining—since I used to like comparing Japan to Taiwan in my videos, like how I once compared Kyushu to Taiwan—if we look at New Taipei City, it’s like the three prefectures surrounding Tokyo. New Taipei is, well, it's like three counties combined,. because New Taipei surrounds Taipei. >> It has both mountains and the sea, and I don't know if you've thought about this, if you often travel to Japan, >> Look, I always keep mine covered. It’s no wonder, your mobile phone wallpaper is a map of New Taipei City. >> Let me tell you a secret, I also used a New Taipei City map as my computer desktop background before. >> Exactly, exactly. No, I think, I think it’s about finding that sense of belonging, which is why we talked about treating this place as home earlier. Right, back to what I was saying, I’ve been making comparisons, so has. everyone noticed that around Tokyo, there’s Chiba Prefecture, Saitama Prefecture, and Kanagawa Prefecture? These are all places that many Taiwanese people love to visit. >> That's right. Take Kanagawa Prefecture for example, since it’s closer to the sea, so simply put, if there’s a comparison to be made, Tamsui could correspond to Yokohama. Some might think, shouldn’t Yokohama correspond to Keelung? No, no, no. Actually, if you look at the earliest ports of the capital, Tamsui should correspond to. Yokohama. >> And then, they have an ancient city called Kamakura, plus another train line that everyone loves to ride and take photos of—the Enoden line. What I want to discuss with you is, how should New Taipei City correspond to these Japanese prefectures and cities in the future? For instance, during your interpellation, you mentioned that the Jiufen-Jinguashi bus route has 5.92 million passengers a year, while I’ve participated in the Crown North Coast route, which only has 38,000. It’s.

# 北海岸交通：直達車與新皇冠計畫

clearly a wonderful place, so how can this be resolved? >> I think it’s like this—you’ve really touched upon exactly what I want to do most. >> As everyone is likely aware, I have another role as a candidate for Mayor of New Taipei City, so I will frankly report to everyone that my policy vision is regional balance and city identity. Regional balance is my ideal, and achieving city identity is my vision. Because there is regional. balance, everyone will identify with the city; there is actually a coherent context to this. Right, so regional balance lies in the fact that our 29 districts in New Taipei City are, in my opinion, all different. They differ in history, culture, landscape, customs, and industrial needs. >> So you must adapt to local conditions and develop according to the local situation. Therefore, we have cities, villages, mountains, and the seaside. So as a New Taipei City team, from the. leaders and grassroots civil servants to the citizens themselves, I really feel we shouldn't just think about heading into Taipei City. >> Instead, even if my job is still currently in Taipei City, >> for my weekends and my time after work, can I stay in New Taipei City to fulfill my living needs, while also letting people from Taipei, or even most other people, come to my area and fall in love with it? That is our real. ambition! What this means is going from being satellites orbiting Taipei City to becoming 29 individual stars. So, " shining bright," that is the vision for New Taipei's future: satellites becoming stars, making New Taipei shine . So, for example, why would they be willing to come here? I think the first step is to create unique features. >> That is why I proposed the New Crown Coast project. >> Yeah. >> It covers my eight coastal townships, yeah. >> It really runs from Bali, Tamsui, Sanzhi, Shimen, all the way to Gongliao. . Right. >> 28 fishing ports, 145 kilometers of coastline, right? Once you organize the fishing ports, first and foremost, you mustn't neglect the fishing industry; it still needs to run smoothly. >> Yes. >> But then you can start developing the tourism that everyone likes now, plus near-shore marine experiences, coastal activities, and even have " all-transport" tourism. What does " all-transport" mean? It’s what everyone is familiar with: cars, buses, and bicycles. Right. >> Scooters and heavy motorcycles—I think heavy motorcycles are great now,. too. >> Yes, they also need places to go. >> Yes, I actually tried riding a heavy motorcycle for a short distance, and I found it quite comfortable, really comfortable. Yes, yes, yes. Okay, but you look at what we've all said—where are the details? The details are just like you said. >> Mm. >> Why does the Jiufen bus line have so many people, and why does the current Crown Coast line have so few? >> I think the difference lies in whether there are direct routes. Oh, direct routes. >> I think that's very important, yes. >> You see, after we conducted this. research and analysis, you realize that when there is a direct route, it often happens at a more mature attraction; and when a relatively mature attraction is paired with a direct route, it's like adding wings to a tiger. >> Truly, truly. >> So for everyone, places like Baishawan or others, if I want to go there and there are only buses that stop occasionally, honestly, it lowers my willingness to go. Right. >> So can we use, say, since my word isn't objective enough, big data analysis or. AI analysis to identify mature or potential attractions, and then increase or adjust bus frequencies? >> It’s about making buses a more comfortable form of public transportation. And it's the same for bicycles; right now everyone just talks about bike lanes, right? No, that’s not how it works now. For bicycles, the focus should be on getting people to stop. >> Yes. >> The key is having the opportunity to stop. Exactly. If you just build a lane , they might just ride right through. >> That's just exercise, just riding 40 or 50 kilometers. We need air stations and smart parking racks so they can safely park their expensive bikes worth over 100,000 or 200,000 NTD. >> Right? When they stop, they can rest and sightsee, and secondly, local businesses get a chance to make sales. So this is moving from point-to-point to a comprehensive approach; this is what I think is different from the past . We are thinking about the tourism policy for the entire North Coast and Northeast Corner in a very detailed and comprehensive way. Of course, there are. other places; I’m already speaking at double speed—you’re not watching at 2 x—but I still feel like I can’t finish. >> Very complete. That’s why I felt I shouldn't interrupt. I didn't want to cut in because that part was so well-stated. Between us, I actually once wrote a sci-fi novel—this isn't in the outline—but what I mean is... >> I imagined that in a parallel universe, our North Coast could have something like the Enoden—the Enoshima Electric Railway—a railway line stretching all. the way from Tamsui to Keelung, which would solve transportation for every location. So, like you just said, while expecting to build a new railway right now might be unrealistic...For the North Coast, indeed, adding rail infrastructure would likely take a much longer time. So, we shouldn't give up on any ideas, but I think the existing things that can be adjusted immediately should be done first to help the area develop again. So for the North Coast,. I advocate for comprehensive tourism, but regarding the railway you just mentioned, it is extremely important for my "Diamond Mountain-City" concept. I was just about to ask about the mountain cities, because aside from the ocean, there are five mountain townships. >> Right, we were just talking about Tokyo ; since Tokyo is situated along a bay, it has that ocean aspect, which we can compare to our North Coast. >> But in fact, it also has mountains.

# 鑽石山城與「新北五道」

>> And to be honest, strictly speaking, New Taipei City seems to have more mountains than ocean. I have eight coastal towns and five mountain towns, but New Taipei City’s forest cover exceeds 70%, the highest among the six special municipalities. >> Really? >> Yes, I was surprised myself after I looked it up, because you don't really feel it. >> Because the general impression is that it's hot and lacks trees, right? >> Yes, or maybe people think Kaohsiung has more, because Kaohsiung...Our forest coverage reached 70%, the. highest among the six cities, but it’s all in the mountain regions. Our mountain area is very large, including Pinglin, Pingxi, Shuangxi, and Wulai— these five are the mountain regions. >> It is truly beautiful. Last time, I went to walk in Pingxi myself, including the hiking trails at Xiaozi Mountain. >> That day happened to be just after it had rained the day before. >> Oh. >> And you can just imagine that green. >> That shade of green is incredible; you. can see how amazing nature is. How can there be so many different shades of green? >> It really is a magical thing. So when I talk about the mountain regions, I refer to New Taipei's "Five Paths": the hiking trail, the railway, the tea path , the mining path, and the old street. Within my mountain regions, I have the hiking trails that people already walk on. The railway and mining/tea paths— well, let's say the trails and railways are for transportation, the mining and. tea paths are historical remains, and the old streets are our current business models. Combining these five, you have different ways to explore from the past to the present, each with its own story. I think stories bring out so many charming aspects; so yes. >> It depends on how you want to play. In the past, many people called me a travel expert, so they would always ask me how domestic tourism should be developed. I certainly pride myself on having a lot of ideas, but honestly, what you just mentioned about mining. tunnels and old streets is something I hadn't really thought about before. >> I brought some photos, can I share them ? Yes, sure, let's take a look. >> Go ahead and share. >> Let me see. Look, this is our railway, our Pingxi line. >> The Pingxi line train was originally built for transporting coal, just like I mentioned with Shulin, it was for coal, which is why those train stations were opened there. Now, many of them, like Pingxi Station or even Jingtong Station, are over a hundred years old, so they actually look beautiful in photos.

# 照片導覽：從平溪、坪林到卯澳灣
